Bekleyiş sonunda sona erdi ve artık bir sonraki James Bond'un kim olduğunu biliyoruz.
2021 yapımı "No Time To Die" filminde Daniel Craig'in (hayli kalıcı) veda performansının ardından yıllarca süren spekülasyonların sonrasında, yedinci 007'yi Robert Pattinson canlandıracak .
İngiliz oyuncu, bu çok arzulanan rol için Jack Lowden, Callum Turner, Josh O'Connor, Nicholas Hoult ve Jacob Elordi gibi isimleri geride bıraktı ve Bond olarak seçilen muhtemelen şimdiye kadarki en ünlü oyuncu oluyor.
Her şeyden önce Pattinson, bugün çalışmakta olan en ilginç ve en çok yönlü A-list yıldızlardan biri olduğu söylenebileceği için 007 için akıllıca bir seçim.
"Harry Potter ve Ateş Kadehi" ve "Alacakaranlık" serisindeki çıkış rollerinden bu yana, artık 40 yaşında olan İngiliz yıldız, sadece gençlik idoli olmadığını kanıtlamak için çok çalıştı.
Projelerini ve yönetmenlerini akıllıca seçerek David Cronenberg (Cosmopolis), James Gray (The Lost City of Z), Claire Denis (High Life), Robert Eggers (The Lighthouse), Safdie kardeşler (Good Time), Bong Joon Ho ( Mickey 17 ), Lynne Ramsay ( Die My Love ) ve Christopher Nolan ( Tenet , The Odyssey ) gibi büyük isimlerle çalıştı. Tüm bu filmler, Pattinson'ın bukalemunu andıran, zaman zaman da eksantrik bir ekran varlığı olduğunu ve açıkça her role girebilecek oyunculuk yeteneğine sahip bulunduğunu gösterdi.
2026'yı ele alalım; Pattinson için başarıların ardı ardına geldiği bir yıl oldu: The Drama , The Odyssey , Primetime ... Üstelik henüz Dune: Part Three'ü izlemedik bile; ki filmin yönetmeni, adı henüz açıklanmayan Bond 26'yı da yöneten Denis Villeneuve.
Bu güçlü kariyer geçmişi, Pattinson'ın James Bond karakterine kendi yorumunu katması ve rolün hakkını vermesi için önemli bir fırsat sunuyor.
Bununla birlikte, oyuncu seçiminin tartışma yaratabilecek yönüne de bakalım: Pattinson bu rol için fazla mı büyük bir yıldız? Sonuçta kendisi zaten bir megastar, hâlâ Bruce Wayne, yani Batman karakterini canlandırıyor ve “The Batman Part II”nin çekimleri de devam ediyor.
Peki, Kara Şövalye'yi canlandıran bir oyuncu aynı zamanda James Bond olabilir mi? Bond rolünün bugüne kadar çoğunlukla oyuncuların kariyerinde bir sıçrama tahtası olduğu, tersinin ise pek görülmediği düşünülürse bu seçim biraz fazla iddialı görünebilir.
Sean Connery, Bond rolünden önce görece tanınmayan bir isimdi. George Lazenby'nin birkaç reklam dışında oyunculuk deneyimi yoktu. Roger Moore, “The Saint” dizisi sayesinde televizyon izleyicisinin aşina olduğu bir oyuncuydu ancak sinemada henüz büyük bir çıkış yakalamamıştı. Timothy Dalton güçlü bir tiyatro kariyerine sahipti ama yerleşik bir sinema yıldızı değildi. Pierce Brosnan ise yıllarca Bond rolü için adı geçen isimlerden biri olsa da esas olarak “Remington Steele” dizisiyle tanınıyordu.
Daniel Craig'in “Road to Perdition”, “Layer Cake” ve “Munich” gibi filmlerde dikkat çeken rolleri vardı. Ancak onu gerçek anlamda başrol oyuncusu konumuna taşıyan yapım “Casino Royale” oldu.
Pattinson ise bu isimlerden farklı bir noktada. Hâlihazırda güvenilir, gişede karşılığı olan bir başrol oyuncusu. Henüz kendini kanıtlayacağı alanlar bulunsa da A-list yıldız statüsünü ve güçlü gişe çekim gücünü çoktan ortaya koymuş durumda.
Bununla birlikte, Pattinson'ın seçilmesi beraberinde oldukça güvenli bir tercih yapıldığı yorumunu da getiriyor.
“Bond 26”, Amazon'un seriyi uzun yıllar yöneten yapımcılar Barbara Broccoli ve Michael G. Wilson'dan devralmasının ardından hayata geçirilecek ilk Bond filmi olacak. Şirketin, serinin bu yeni döneminde doğru isimlerle yola çıktığını kanıtlaması gerekiyor.
Eski Bond geleneği düşünüldüğünde Pattinson'ın seçilmesi pek olası görünmezdi. Genellikle henüz kariyerinin yükseliş aşamasındaki bir oyuncuya verilen rolün bu kez zaten küresel bir yıldıza emanet edilmesi, Amazon'un risk almak istemediğine işaret ediyor. Şirket, yatırımının karşılığını almak ve tıpkı “Skyfall” gibi bir sonraki Bond filminin de 1 milyar dolarlık gişe başarısına ulaşmasını hedefliyor. Pattinson'ın seçimi ve yönetmen tercihi de bu beklentiyi güçlendiriyor.
Nitekim Denis Villeneuve, bugüne kadar bir Bond filmi yönetmek üzere seçilen en heyecan verici isimlerden biri. Oscar adayı yönetmen, “Incendies”den “Prisoners”a, “Sicario”dan “Arrival”a ve “Blade Runner 2049”a uzanan filmografisinde farklı türlerdeki başarısını ortaya koydu. Frank Herbert'in uzun süre sinemaya uyarlanması zor kabul edilen “Dune” romanlarını da yeni kuşağın büyük bilimkurgu serilerinden birine dönüştürdü.
Buna bir de “Eastern Promises” ve “Locke” filmlerinin senaristi; “Peaky Blinders”, “Taboo”, “SAS: Rogue Heroes” ve “The Veil” dizilerinin yaratıcısı ve yazarı Steven Knight'ın senaryoya imza atacağını ekleyin. Tüm bu isimler bir araya geldiğinde, gişede büyük başarı hedefleyen iddialı bir Bond filmi ortaya çıkıyor.
Beklentilerin bu denli yükseldiği bir ortamda, bir sonraki Bond filminin bu beklentileri karşılaması gerekecek. Üstelik James Bond'u canlandırmak, beraberinde ciddi bir incelemeyi ve yoğun tartışmaları da getiriyor.
Pattinson'ın seçimi bazı izleyicileri oldukça memnun ederken, diğerleri aynı fikirde değil.
Aslında bu tepkiler yeni değil. Sean Connery Bond rolünü üstlendiğinde, izleyicilerin çoğu karakteri Cary Grant'in canlandırmasını istiyordu. Timothy Dalton seçildiğinde ise Pierce Brosnan'ın televizyon dizisi “Remington Steele” nedeniyle rolü alamamış olması hayal kırıklığı yaratmıştı. Daniel Craig'in adı açıklandığında da eleştiriler gecikmedi: Fazla kısa, fazla sıradan ve fazla sarışın bulunmuştu. Ancak “Casino Royale”, bu itirazları dile getirenlere zamanla yanıldıklarını gösterdi.
Şimdi ise Pattinson'ın Bond seçilmesine gelen tepkilere bakalım. İşte en iyi, en komik, en coşkulu ve en alıngan yorumlardan bazıları. Üstelik listeye herhangi bir izleyicinin değil, doğrudan Kraliyet Ailesi'nin resmî paylaşımıyla başlıyoruz:
“2008'de birine, Twilight'taki Edward'ın yıllar sonra hem James Bond hem de Batman olacağını ve herkesin bu seçimden memnun kalacağını söyleseydiniz ne derdi acaba? Ne tuhaf ama bir o kadar da eğlenceli bir kariyer yolculuğu!”
"Twilight resmen Robert Pattinson'ın James Bond olacağını önceden söyledi bu arada."
"Harry Potter. Twilight. Tenet. The Batman. The Odyssey. Primetime. Dune. Ve şimdi JAMES BOND. Cedric Diggory'den Bruce Wayne'e, oradan 007'ye. ROBERT PATTINSON."
"Batman'i VE Bond'u oynamak, İncil'de bahsedilen türden bir açgözlülük; ama rolü Villeneuve'ün yönettiği Pattinson Bond'unda başka kimseyi görmek isteyebileceğimi hayal bile edemiyorum. Villeneuve imzalı Pattinson Bond'u çarpıcı olacak."
Bu seçime çok sevinmeyen sosyal medya kullanıcıları da vardı.
“James Bond zarif, sofistike, son derece zeki ve çelik gibi sağlam olmalı. Her erkeğin onun gibi olmak, her kadının da onunla birlikte olmak isteyeceği biri olmalı. Robert Pattinson, 007 değil! Üstelik berbat bir Batman'di.”
“Aptalca bir karar. Robert Pattinson, Bond rolü için doğru isim değil. Üstelik mükemmel adayı bulmuşken onu elinizden kaçırdınız. BU SEÇİMDEN NEFRET EDİYORUM.”
"James Bond'un Robert Pattinson tarafından canlandırılmasını sevmeyen tek kişi ben miyim? Hep daha az bilinen bir İngiliz oyuncu için kariyer değiştiren bir şey olmasını sevmiştim."
“Robert Pattinson'ın James Bond olarak seçilmesi, hayal gücünden yoksun bir karar. Birincisi, Pattinson zaten Batman'i canlandırıyor. Gerçekten oyuncu kıtlığı mı yaşanıyor da bütün ikonik karakterleri aynı birkaç oyuncunun üstlenmesi gerekiyor? İkincisi, Pattinson bu role beraberinde fazlasıyla tanınırlık ve geçmiş rol çağrışımı getiriyor. Bond'u canlandıran oyuncular, karakterle özdeşleşmeleri sayesinde tanınan, izleyicinin zihninde henüz belirli bir imajı olmayan isimler olmalı; onlarca yıllık çağrışımları beraberinde getiren yerleşik sinema yıldızları değil.”
Tüm bu tepkilere rağmen, 2028'de “Bond 26” vizyona girene kadar tartışmaların nasıl sonuçlanacağını bilemeyeceğiz. Filmin resmî gösterim tarihi henüz açıklanmadı. Pattinson'ın 007'ye nasıl bir yorum getireceğini ve bu rolü kendine özgü kılıp kılamayacağı…

İYİ Parti; Milli Dayanışma, Kardeşlik ve Demokrasi Komisyonu'na üye vermemişti ve Milli Dayanışma ve Toplumsal Bütünleşmenin Güçlendirilmesine Dair Kanun Teklifi'ne ise hayır oyu vermişti.
Dervişoğlu, teklifin gerçek anlamda TBMM tarafından hazırlanmadığını savunmuş ve Genel Kurul konuşmasında “Bu kanun teklifini TBMM mi hazırlamıştır ki onun onayına sunulmaktadır?” demişti.
Kurtulmuş yarın, Yeni Parti Grubu'nu ziyaret edip Genel Başkan Özgür Özel ile görüşecek.
10 Kasım'da Meclis'te siyasi parti liderlerini ve siyasi parti gruplarını ziyarete başlayan TBMM Başkanı'nın ilk durağı CHP olmuştu.
Yaklaşık 40 dakika süren görüşme basına kapalı gerçekleştirilmiş ve Milli Dayanışma ve Toplumsal Bütünleşmenin Güçlendirilmesine Dair Kanun kapsamında TBMM'de kurulacak İzleme Komisyonu hakkında fikir alışverişinde bulunulduğu öğrenilmişti.
Kılıçdaroğlu ile görüşmesinin ardından aynı gün Yeni Yol Grubu ile görüşen Kurtulmuş, ziyaretin ardından basın mensupların açıklamalarda bulunup terörsüz Türkiye sürecinde TBMM'de yaklaşık bir yıldır devam eden çalışmalarda olumlu bir noktaya geldiklerini belirtmişti.
"Fikirler olgunlaşacak, önümüzdeki hafta da görüşmeleri tamamlayacağız." diye konuşan Kurtulmuş, "En kısa süre içinde TBMM'de oluşturulacak izleme komisyonu, millet adına bu süreci takip ve kontrol etmek için çalışmalarına başlayacaktır." demişti.
Kurtulmuş, 11 Kasım'da ise AK Parti Grup Başkanı Abdullah Güler ile görüştü.
Yine Meclis'te basına kapalı gerçekleşen görüşme, yaklaşık 40 dakika sürdü.
Görüşmede, AK Parti Genel Başkan Yardımcısı Hüseyin Yayman, Grup Başkanvekilleri Abdulhamit Gül, Özlem Zengin, Leyla Şahin Usta, Bahadır Yenişehirlioğlu ile Muhammet Emin Akbaşoğlu da yer aldı.
Görüşmenin ardından gazetecilere açıklamalarda bulunan AK Parti Grup Başkanı Güler, Kurtulmuş'un komisyona yönelik AK Parti TBMM Grubu'nun görüşünü aldığını aktarıp şöyle konuşmuştu:
“Kanunun adı, Milli Dayanışma ve Toplumsal Bütünleşmenin Güçlendirilmesine Dair Kanun. İzleme komisyonun adı da Kanunla beraber yer alacaktır. TBMM nezdinde, Milli Dayanışma ve Toplumsal Bütünleşmenin Güçlendirilmesine Dair İzleme Komisyonudur. Biz fikirlerimizi beyan ettik. Diğer parti grupları da beyan edecektir, ondan sonra ortaya bir tablo ortaya çıkacaktır.”
12 Kasım'da Bahçeli ile görüşen Kurtulmuş'un ziyareti ise 40 dakika sürdü.

AFAD koordinasyonunda deprem uzmanlarından oluşan 20 kişilik ekip, 6 Şubat 2023'teki depremlerde kırılmayan Suriye'deki fayları mercek altına aldı.
Türkiye ve Suriye'nin farklı üniversitelerinde görev yapan deprem uzmanları , Maden Tetkik ve Arama Genel Müdürlüğü ile AFAD Deprem ve Risk Azaltma Genel Müdürlüğü yetkilileri, Suriye'deki fay hatlarının bulunduğu bölgelerde çalışmalara başladı.
Türkiye ekibinde AFAD Deprem ve Risk Azaltma Genel Müdürü Prof. Dr. Orhan Tatar koordinatörlüğünde yürütülen çalışmaya Dokuz Eylül Üniversitesi Deprem Araştırma ve Uygulama Merkezi Müdürü Prof. Dr. Hasan Sözbilir, Eskişehir Osmangazi Üniversitesinden Prof. Dr. Volkan Karabacak ve MTA'dan Hasan Elmacı katıldı.
Ölü Deniz Fayı ile bağlantılı bir kısmı Türkiye'de yer alan Yesemek, Hacıpaşa ve Reyhanlı fayları ile Suriye topraklarındaki Afrin, Sarmada ve Armanaz fayları ekipler tarafından incelendi.
Çalışmalara katılan AFAD Deprem Bilim Kurulu Üyesi Prof. Dr. Hasan Sözbilir, AA muhabirine, Türkiye ve Suriye arasında depremsellik ve fayların tanınması için çok kapsamlı çalışma başlatıldığını söyledi.
6 Şubat depremlerinde Türkiye tarafındaki fayların önemli bir kısmının kırıldığını hatırlatan Sözbilir, "Asrın felaketi sonrası komşumuz Suriye'deki sınır ötesi faylarda henüz bir kırılma gerçekleşmedi. Dolayısıyla bu fayların tarih öncesi deprem geçmişini ortaya koymak için bir çalışma yaptık. Öncelikle Afrin, Armanaz ve Sarmada fayları üzerinde arazide inceleme yaptık. Oradaki fayların özelliklerine göre farklı kesimlerinde hendek yerlerini belirledik. Bir sonraki gelişimizde bu faylar üzerinde belli ölçeklerde hendek açacağız. Böylece gelecekte ve yakın dönemde bu fayların depremselliğini ortaya koymuş olacağız." diye konuştu.
Sözbilir, deprem ve yer bilimi konusunda uzman isimlerle Suriye'de 5 gün boyunca fayları incelediklerini dile getirdi.
Fayların bir kısmının Türkiye'den geçtiğini belirten Sözbilir, şunları kaydetti:
"Yarısı bizim tarafta, yarısı Suriye'de olan faylar var. Kilis'ten güneye doğru inen faylar var. Bunlar Ölü Deniz Fayı'nın segmentleri aslında. Ölü Deniz Fay zonu, Kahramanmaraş'tan başlayıp Kızıldeniz'e kadar uzanan yaklaşık 1000 kilometre uzunluğundaki bir fay. Bu fayların önemli bir bölümü 500 ila 2000 yıldır kırılmamış görünüyor. Dolayısıyla bizim için yakın gelecekte kırılma tehlikesi olan faylar hangileri bunları bilmek istiyoruz. Bu faylar son depremi ne zaman yaptı? Ne kadar vaktimiz var, tüm bunları öğrenmek istiyoruz. Türkiye ve Suriye arasındaki faylar bu şekilde ilk kez inceleniyor. Fayları bilimsel olarak tanımaya çalışıyoruz."
AFAD'ın belirleyeceği takvime göre yeniden bölgeye gideceklerini dile getiren Prof. Dr. Sözbilir, yerinde gözlem yaptıkları her fay üzerinde en az ikişer hendek yeri saptadıklarını ifade etti.
20-30 metre eninde ve 3-4 metre derinliğinde hendekler açacaklarını anlatan Sözbilir, "Fayın geçmişini göreceğiz, örnekler toplayacağız, onlar analize gidecek. Elde edeceğimiz verilere göre fayların eski depremlere ait kayıtlarını ortaya çıkaracağız. Tüm bunların ardından bölgedeki fayların Suriye ve Türkiye için ne kadar tehlike oluşturacağı belirlenmiş olacak." diye konuştu.
Türkiye ve dünyadaki en güncel gelişmelerden haberdar olmak için, bültenlerin gönderileceği e-posta adresini girin.

Türkiye ve Suriye’nin çeşitli üniversitelerinden akademisyenlerin yanı sıra Maden Tetkik ve Arama Genel Müdürlüğü (MTA) ve AFAD yetkililerinin yer aldığı heyette; Dokuz Eylül Üniversitesi Deprem Araştırma ve Uygulama Merkezi Müdürü Prof. Dr. Hasan Sözbilir, Eskişehir Osmangazi Üniversitesinden Prof. Dr. Volkan Karabacak ve MTA'dan Hasan Elmacı yer aldı.

Çalışmalara ilişkin değerlendirmelerde bulunan AFAD Deprem Bilim Kurulu Üyesi Prof. Dr. Hasan Sözbilir, Türkiye ve Suriye arasındaki fayların tarih öncesi deprem geçmişini ortaya çıkarmak için ilk kez bu kapsamda ortak bir çalışma yürütüldüğünü vurguladı.
6 Şubat depremlerinde Türkiye tarafındaki fayların önemli bir kısmının kırıldığını hatırlatan Prof. Dr. Sözbilir, sınır ötesindeki tehlikeye şu sözlerle dikkat çekti:

Yarısı bizim tarafta, yarısı Suriye'de olan, Kilis'ten güneye doğru inen faylar var. Bunlar Kahramanmaraş'tan başlayıp Kızıldeniz'e kadar uzanan yaklaşık 1000 kilometre uzunluğundaki Ölü Deniz Fay zonunun segmentleri. Bu fayların önemli bir bölümü 500 ila 2000 yıldır kırılmamış görünüyor. Dolayısıyla bizim için yakın gelecekte kırılma tehlikesi olan faylar hangileri bunları bilmek istiyoruz. Bu faylar son depremi ne zaman yaptı? Ne kadar vaktimiz var, tüm bunları öğrenmek istiyoruz."
Arazi gözlemleri sırasında her fay üzerinde en az ikişer hendek yeri tespit ettiklerini belirten Sözbilir, AFAD'ın belirleyeceği takvim doğrultusunda bölgeye yeniden gidileceğini ifade etti. İkinci aşamada fay hatları üzerinde 20-30 metre eninde ve 3-4 metre derinliğinde hendekler açılacağını aktaran Sözbilir, toplanacak örneklerin analiziyle fayların eski depremlere ait kayıtlarının ortaya çıkarılacağını ve bölgenin Türkiye ile Suriye açısından taşıdığı tehlike boyutunun netleşeceğini kaydetti.

Sinema dünyasının yıllardır merakla beklediği yeni James Bond 'un kim olacağı sorusu yanıt buldu. Amazon MGM Studios, efsanevi 007 karakterini İngiliz oyuncu Robert Pattinson'ın canlandıracağını duyurdu. Alacakaranlık ve The Batman filmleriyle dünya çapında ün kazanan 40 yaşındaki oyuncu, Daniel Craig'den boşalan koltuğun yeni sahibi oldu.
2021 yapımı Ölmek İçin Zaman Yok filmiyle Daniel Craig'in James Bond macerasının sona ermesinin ardından gözler yeni oyuncunun kim olacağına çevrilmişti. Uzun süren oyuncu seçme sürecinin sonunda yapım şirketi tercihini Robert Pattinson'dan yana kullandı.
Pattinson böylece Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan ve Daniel Craig'in ardından James Bond'u canlandıracak yedinci oyuncu oldu.
Yeni rolüne ilişkin açıklama yapan Robert Pattinson, James Bond'un sinema tarihinin en efsanevi karakterlerinden biri olduğunu belirterek 007 rolünün kendisine emanet edilmesini hayatının en büyük onurlarından biri olarak nitelendirdi.
Ünlü oyuncu, bu rolün kendisi için bir hayalin gerçekleşmesi anlamına geldiğini ifade ederek yeni projede yer almaktan büyük heyecan duyduğunu söyledi.
James Bond serisinin 26. filmini Dune ve Arrival gibi yapımlarla tanınan Denis Villeneuve yönetecek. Senaryoyu ise Peaky Blinders dizisinin yaratıcısı Steven Knight kaleme alacak.
Filmin yapımcılığını Amy Pascal ve David Heyman üstlenecek. Henüz adı ve vizyon tarihi açıklanmayan yapım, Amazon MGM Studios'un yaratıcı kontrolünde hazırlanacak ilk James Bond filmi olacak.
Roger Moore sonrası Bond oyuncuları tam bir fiyasko. Özellikle Daniel Craig’le başlayan çöküntü Robert Pattinson’la zirve yaptı. Bond’un asil, çapkın ve karizmatik görüntüsü yok edildi!

Airline acknowledges ‘technology issue that delayed flight departures’ in latest high-profile outage to affect Americans
United ⁠Airlines said on ⁠Monday ⁠that it had resolved ⁠a widespread system ⁠outage, just three days after the Federal ⁠Aviation Administration issued a rare nationwide ground stop on all US flights.
“We have resolved a technology issue that delayed flight departures. While some flights were delayed, there was no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights,” Chicago-based United said in a statement. “There is no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue.”
According to an internal memo from ​United’s pilots’ ‌union seen ‌by Reuters, a company-wide ‌web-based outage had affected multiple applications used by pilots, including crew communications. It said United was unable to provide final ‌aircraft weights for departing flights and advised pilots to ​follow airport station guidance on whether to leave their gates.
Before every departure, pilots use performance software, often on a cockpit tablet, to check that the aircraft can safely take off under current weather and runway conditions. The preflight calculations include the aircraft’s weight along with information about the fuel, baggage, cargo and passengers the plane is carrying.
Sean Duffy, the US transportation secretary, said in an interview Monday night that he did not know what caused the one-and-a-half-hour outage. “This is not ‌an FAA [Federal Aviation Administration] system-wide problem,” Duffy said on Hannity on Fox News.
The United computer issue is just the latest high-profile technology meltdown to affect Americans in the last few days. On Friday, ageing equipment led to a temporary grounding of all commercial airplanes in the US for more than four hours, sparking travel chaos as thousands of flights were delayed or canceled.
Airlines have experienced similar disruptions before. ‌In August 2025, United temporarily grounded flights after a problem with its Unimatic system, which supplies flight information to systems used to calculate aircraft weight and balance. It was not immediately clear whether Monday’s outage ​involved United’s Unimatic system.
The Trump administration said the rare ground stop stemmed from a fiber upgrade during routine maintenance that led to data flooding, which crashed a critical communication system.
And earlier on Monday, customers reported service outages and difficulty accessing their online accounts at several major US banks and the money transfer service Zelle after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system.
It also comes after a major outage by Microsoft that began on Thursday and lasted into the next day, which crippled a host of services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot. The outage had serious repercussions for millions of people and organizations all over the world, including schools, hospitals, businesses, courts, banks, prisons, police forces and governments.
Microsoft said it had resolved the issue and restored service by Saturday, also issuing an apology. The office software giant did not attribute the blackout to a cybersecurity breach, identifying in an initial report on Monday that a combination of a months-old bug, malfunctioning internal connections, and server capacity sparked the outage.

Kentte düzenlenen Birleşmiş Milletler İklim Değişikliği Çerçeve Sözleşmesi 31. Taraflar Konferansı (COP31) kapsamında, Antalya Valiliği, Antalya Büyükşehir Belediyesi ve Antalya Tarım Konseyi (ATAK) arasındaki mutabakat için Yeşil Bölge'deki Antalya Evi'nde tören gerçekleştirildi.
Vali Şahin, törende yaptığı konuşmada, COP31'in uygulama odaklı olacağını belirterek, imzalanan mutabakatın da bunun önemli bir örneği olduğunu söyledi.
Antalya'nın bir tarım şehri olduğunun altını çizen Şahin, kentin Türkiye'nin en büyük, dünyada da sayılı tarım üretim merkezlerinden biri olduğunu belirtti.
İklim değişikliğinin birinci derecede etkilediği sektör olan tarımın da yeni düzene hazırlanması gerektiğini vurgulayan Şahin, şunları kaydetti:
"Artık eski usul tarım yöntemleriyle​​​​​​​ devam edebilme şansımız kalmadı. Artık yeni sözler, yeni uygulama yöntemleri tespit etmeli ve bunları uygulamalıyız. Bu su yönetiminden tohum kullanımına, yeni tip seralardan yağmur hasadına, atık yönetimine kadar çok geniş çaplı bir uygulamayı beraberinde getiriyor. Bu mutabakatla Antalya çiftçileri, Antalya'da tarım konusundaki bileşenler, tarım konusundaki paydaşlar şunu ifade ediyorlar, 'Biz iklim değişikliğinin bize getirdiği yeni tarım yöntemlerine hazırlıklıyız, bunun için elimizden geleni yapacağız'."
Şahin, su kullanımından ilaca ve gübreye kadar tarımın tamamını sürdürülebilir hale getirebilmek, çevreye duyarlı bir tarım yapabilmek için tarafların mutabakata imza attıklarını ifade etti.

Bu çerçevede 30'u aşkın toplantı yaptıklarını ve 7 ana maddede 31 başlıkta Antalya tarımının iklimle mücadelesini öngörecek bir anlaşmaya vardıklarını dile getiren Çandır, "Burada yaptığımız işleyen kamu kurumlarının, özel sektörün işlerine müdahale değil, aksine onların işlerini kolaylaştırıcı, destek verici bir çalışmadır." dedi.
Antalya Büyükşehir Belediye Başkan Vekili Büşra Özdemir de mutabakatın hayırlı olmasını diledi.

Meta, Instagram 'ın mesajlaşma bölümünü Direct adlı bağımsız bir uygulama olarak test etmeye başladı. Android ve iOS için sunulan uygulama şimdilik yalnızca Türkiye ve Tayland'da deneniyor. Instagram hesabı olanlar kullanıcı adı ve şifreleriyle giriş yapabiliyor, sohbetler iki uygulama arasında eşitleniyor; hesabı olmayanlar ise telefon numarası veya e-postayla kaydolabiliyor.
Türkçe arayüzle yayımlanan giriş ekranlarında Direct, ' Instagram 'ın bir mesajlaşma uygulaması' olarak tanıtılıyor. Başlamak için Instagram mesajlarının ve profil bilgilerinin uygulamada görüneceği belirtiliyor. Arkadaşlara Direct'ten ya da Instagram'dan mesaj gönderilebiliyor; karşı tarafın hangi uygulamayı kullandığı fark etmiyor. Ekranlardaki bir uyarı da dikkat çekiyor: Direct'i kullanmak, kapatılmış bir Instagram profilini geri yüklemeyecek.
Bildirim ekranında ise hem Direct'ten hem Instagram'dan mesaj ve kişi bildirimi alınacağı söyleniyor. Bu tercih Ayarlar'dan istendiği zaman değiştirilebiliyor. Giriş için 'Meta Hesabıyla devam et' seçeneği kullanılıyor.
Uygulamanın içinde yaratıcı araçlar da var. Sohbet penceresinde çizim yapılabiliyor (Draw), gelen kutusunun üstünde kısa durum notları paylaşılabiliyor (Notes). Özelleştirilebilir çıkartmalar, sesli mesajlar için efektler ve sohbet arka planını değiştiren temalar da listede yer alıyor.
Meta'nın paylaştığı görselde Direct'in gelen kutusu, Instagram 'daki mesaj ekranına çok benziyor. En üstte arkadaşların kısa notları sıralanıyor, altında bire bir ve grup sohbetleri geliyor. Hesabı olmayan kullanıcılar için kurallar daha sıkı: Yalnızca telefon rehberindeki kişilerle sohbet başlatılabiliyor veya gruplara eklenebiliyor. Listeye yeni biri eklemek için tam kullanıcı adını yazmak ya da QR kodu yüz yüze taratmak gerekiyor.
Meta'nın duyurusuna göre 'yalnızca kişileriniz ve zaten bağlantıda olduğunuz kişiler' sizinle sohbet başlatabiliyor. Kullanıcılar istedikleri zaman bir kişiyi engelleyebiliyor, kısıtlayabiliyor, bildirebiliyor ya da listeden kaldırabiliyor. Uygulama için en az 13 yaşında olmak gerekiyor; yaşı doğrulanmayan hesaplar silinecek. Gençlerin uygunsuz etkileşimlerini tespit etmek için özel teknolojiler kullanılacak. Ebeveynler de çocuklarının kiminle yazıştığını görebiliyor, güvenlik ayarlarını yönetebiliyor ve günlük kullanım süresine sınır koyabiliyor.
Direct adı Instagram için yabancı değil. Şirket 2017'de aynı isimle ayrı bir mesajlaşma uygulamasını aralarında Türkiye'nin de bulunduğu birkaç ülkede denemiş, 2019'da bu uygulamayı kapatıp sohbetleri ana uygulamaya geri taşımıştı.

Excepting the few models that look like regular hats, most red-light therapy for hair growth devices look … well, pretty weird. From stormtrooper helmets to headpieces that look like they were designed for Geordi La Forge , these aren’t exactly accessories you’d want to wear in public. Which is why it was nice to unbox the Capillus HairBand and find, at long last, a normal-looking headband.
Discreet black, fabric-covered, and sized like a normal hair accessory, the HairBand’s only indication it might do something more than hold back hair is a little 2 x 1-inch battery pack that sits jauntily cocked to one side. It’s refreshing to finally see a red-light device that doesn’t embarrass the user or frighten animals and young children , but after testing it for over a month, I found the HairBand has its share of shortcomings for the price.
Interestingly, Capillus makes a series of full-coverage devices with laser diodes built into what looks like a normal black baseball cap. However, the cheapest of these hats runs $1,699, and the most expensive “triple-wavelength” model, with 312 laser diodes, runs $3,299. The 2-inch-wide Capillus HairBand provides a similar laser diode treatment for less, at $599 with only 82 diodes (650 nm). (Capillus says the headband is designed to prioritize areas where hair loss is most noticeable, such as the hairline and temples.)
Unlike straight LED lights, laser diodes provide collimated beams of light that travel in a straight line, allowing for more focused and intense treatment of hair follicles. I actually saw some success with this treatment when I tested the HairBand’s closest competitor, Hairmax’s LaserBand 82 ComfortFlex ($849) . It couldn’t help follicles that were scarred or had already died, but studies have shown that red-light therapy can energize follicles that have more recently become dormant.
I did see some growth in the middle of my part with the LaserBand, and while I stopped using it to switch to the HairBand exclusively for the past five or so weeks, I admit this growth did make it difficult to isolate the HairBand’s contribution, especially since the headband’s coverage area is so small. Thus, the following observations are mainly on the wearing experience of the HairBand, not hair growth.
At only 2 inches wide and five minutes per section, the HairBand took at least 15 minutes to cover my entire part, compared with the 3-inch-wide LaserBand, which also only needs to be used three times per week at 30 seconds per section for a total of 90 seconds. I’m a Type-A full-time working parent in my mid-forties, and let me tell you—15 minutes of doing nothing is a long time in my world.
The HairBand has teeth and could sit on my head as long as it was in a normal headband position, right in the middle, but the weight of the battery pack pulls it forward ever so slightly, so if I was leaning over or doing anything that didn’t hold my head exactly straight, it would start to slip off. This meant I had to hold it with my hand, which meant no multitasking.
Capillus’ marketing materials use words like “ritual” and feature pictures of twentysomethings admiring themselves in the mirror, but I can’t imagine these women are suffering from the perimenopausal hair loss that would necessitate use of a red-light device in the first place.
I don’t consider myself to have an overly large head and have never had trouble with hats or other hair accessories, but this headband, which weighs only 6 ounces, felt quite small and somewhat precarious on my head overall. I should note it is also rather overtly feminine in style—my husband and I were able to share “custody” of the LaserBand, but he declined to wear this one, and I didn’t blame him.
There were two other concerns during my testing. One, the back of the box said it contained quick-start instructions, but my box only had the headband and USB-C charging cord—no physical user guide to be found ( except online , but I had to do some googling). Not that one is needed, since it’s pretty obvious how it works—push the start button on the battery pack, and it will beep and shut off when the five minutes are up—but it’s an odd omission at this price point.
Two, this device is not currently FDA-cleared for treating hair loss or promoting regrowth. This isn’t ideal, but FDA-cleared is much different from FDA-approved; it simply requires the manufacturer to prove its product is “substantially equivalent” to an already FDA-cleared product. (And it doesn’t ensure results, just that it’s safe to use as directed.) Capillus’ rep tells me the brand is currently working on the FDA filing for the HairBand, which was released in September of this year, and intends to have it cleared in 2027. (The brand’s cap-style devices are FDA-cleared.) Even so, the HairBand is a unique device in this space, but if I’m spending that much on a red-light device, I would prefer a little more versatility in the design.

The mad scramble to score Imax tickets for The Odyssey was about as intense as the Trojan War, and the Marvel Cinematic Universe showed signs of resurgence with Spider-Man: Brand New Day ’s $2.5 billion global haul. But the biggest buzz of the 2026 summer movie season? Two small-scale horror films from a couple of young YouTube auteurs.
First came Obsession , from 27-year-old Curry Barker, which made more than $500 million worldwide on a budget of less than $1 million. The film follows a meek young man named Bear, who yearns to be in a romantic relationship with his friend Nikki and uses a magical object to make his wish come true. By turns moody, funny, and shocking, Obsession proved that audiences are hungry to talk about something other than reheated IP. Barker got his start with the YouTube sketch comedy channel That’s a Bad Idea, while 21-year-old Kane Parsons gained a cult following on the platform by experimenting with visual effects and creepy atmospherics. A series of short films Parsons made in his teens culminated with the release of Backrooms in May. The feature picked up the narrative from those earlier YouTube videos, which were themselves inspired by an old 4chan meme and internet folklore around the idea of haunted liminal spaces.
Parsons’ avid fandom anticipated a big-screen Backrooms long before he signed with A24, making the movie a guaranteed hit. Backrooms earned $400 million worldwide on a budget of $10 million, surpassing Marty Supreme as the studio’s highest-grossing movie ever. The film stars Chiwetel Ejiofor as Clark, a depressed divorcé who runs a failing furniture warehouse and vents about his ruined marriage to his therapist. One night, when investigating his store’s glitchy electrical system, he stumbles through a wall and into an apparently infinite maze of fluorescent-lit hallways that contain what seem to be deconstructed or misremembered pieces of the real world—and perhaps some living entities as well.
Though Backrooms stands alone as a hallucinatory vision of a vast, ever-expanding unreality just outside our own, many critics also read it as commentary on the state of generative artificial intelligence, which mindlessly reproduces and regurgitates its training data in permutations that often don’t make sense. Whether Parsons intended that interpretation or not, he spoke out against AI several times following the movie’s release, calling it “a symptom of a broader cultural and economic rot.”
Then there’s Zach Cregger. While not a YouTuber per se, he got his start in sketch comedy (The Whitest Kids U’ Know) and this year followed 2025’s Weapons with a 2026 adaptation of Resident Evil .
Parsons told WIRED earlier in the year that he imagines his cohort of directors will bring certain YouTube sensibilities to Hollywood. “I don’t think there’s a lot of Instagram filmmakers or a lot of TikTok filmmakers that go for long-form content in a way that would actually be looked at or respected as film,” he says. “So it feels like YouTube is the only viable avenue in that way, in an actual meaningful mainstream context.” Among the crop of twentysomething filmmakers entering the industry today, “I think it’s very unlikely that you would have a filmmaker who is sort of reaching that place right now and getting that kind of media attention who has not at some point in the last 20 years put stuff on YouTube,” Parsons says.
Studios have certainly taken notice, scouting the site’s horror content for fresh talent and aggressively pursuing breakout projects. After a screening of Barker’s Obsession at the Toronto International Film Festival in 2025, A24 and Neon embarked on a bidding war for the film before it was picked up by Focus Features for roughly $15 million.
Netflix reportedly also lost out on a bid to take Obsession straight to streaming; it’s possible that other young directors will follow Barker’s example in pushing for theatrical release.
The YouTube generation is proving that the internet can supply whatever education you might need on your path to the red carpet. While Hollywood consolidation threatens to stifle creativity, a new wave of artists are betting on themselves—and some are winning.

Rachel Accurso, better known by her stage name Ms. Rachel , specializes in making videos for babies and toddlers. She started as a DIY creator on YouTube , working with her musician husband Aron and shooting around New York on a shoestring budget. To an adult with a fully formed frontal lobe, her videos can be, well, a bit much: a whole lot of close-ups on Accurso’s mouth making shapes, cutesy stomp-clap sessions, and winsome nursery rhymes.
To children, though, the videos are a portal into a temporary bliss state so powerful that many parents have come to view Accurso as a quasi-­mythical figure. She has racked up billions of views and gained so many fervent fans that she inked a juicy deal with Netflix last year, cementing her status as the biggest star in digital children’s entertainment. This fall, she released her first album, I’m So Happy , and she sells a slate of branded toys and picture books. But when people look back on 2026, they’ll likely remember Ms. Rachel for something unrelated to her kid-centric empire: offering an example, for adults, of how to be a good person.
Accurso speaks in a singsong voice when she’s performing in her trademark denim overalls and bubblegum-pink shirt. The former preschool music teacher started out hoping to create videos to help her son communicate, focusing on sign language, repetition, and other strategies employed by language development specialists. The saccharine voice is part of it. Research indicates that speaking in high-pitched, rhythmic patterns best spurs imitations from kids.
But this cotton-candy tone belies the convictions that drive Accurso professionally and personally. She is perhaps the single staunchest celebrity advocate for children and has faced fierce criticism for her advocacy on behalf of Palestinian kids. On her show, she has featured children like Rahaf Saed, a toddler who became a double amputee after an Israeli air strike hit her home in Gaza. At an awards ceremony, Accurso wore a dress embroidered with artwork from Gazan children. Recently, she pledged $1 million to the Palestinian Children’s Relief Fund; she’s gone so far as to insist that all of her collaborators speak on the issue and has called out celebrities who fail to do so.
She’s often compared to Mr. Rogers, but Accurso is as much an inheritor of Jane Fonda’s activist mantle. Blowback to her advocacy has been intense—pro-Israel groups have accused Accurso of antisemitism. One of these groups even wrote to Florida’s attorney general, asking for Accurso to be investigated as a potential “foreign agent” spewing “Hamas-aligned propaganda.” None of this has deterred her from speaking out. “I would risk everything, and I will risk my career over and over to stand up” for kids, she said in a radio interview last year.
Accurso’s willingness to duke it out doesn’t end with Gaza. She has weathered right-wing ire for employing nonbinary performer Jules Hoffman, for celebrating Pride Month, and for speaking out against ICE. She helped draw attention to the plight of a nonverbal 5-year-old imprisoned at a South Texas detention center by featuring a Zoom call with him on her social media. An immigration lawyer saw Accurso’s post and connected with the boy’s family, helping secure his release. “We need to put children’s lives and human lives before our hesitations,” Accurso said in an interview about her activism around ICE detentions. “I just urge everyone, especially those with huge platforms and privilege, to speak out.” For her efforts, Fox News described Accurso as “really sinister.”
Talk to anyone who has encountered Accurso in person and they’re likely to share a glowing story about how lovely she is. I’ll add mine to the pile. A few years ago, when I interviewed her for a story about YouTube and children’s television, I was bleary-eyed on Zoom after a long night with a teething baby. I mentioned that my then 1-year-old adored her videos, especially a song she sings about hopping bunnies, and that I’d sung it to him at night. A few weeks later, I got an email from Accurso. It had a video attached; she’d made my son a personalized sing-along, making sure to say his name repeatedly during the Bunny Hop song so he knew it was something special, just for him.

For our inaugural WIRED Yearbook, we celebrate the people, inventions, and viral moments that made it a little more bearable—and are already defining the future.
ANIMATIONS BY LUKTHIS STUDIO ILLUSTRATIONS AND PHOTO TREATMENT BY ROB VARGAS
An internet devoured by AI . Surveillance at every traffic light. Global leaders who seem determined to bring about dystopia. At the end of a year like 2026, it’s tempting to conclude that there’s little room for idealism. Don’t give in! After all, this year we also saw a new generation of filmmakers challenge Hollywood, teenagers take on AI companies, and scientists make once-unimaginable breakthroughs. We saw activists fight surveillance, astronauts do the impossible, and an adorable raccoon melt the internet’s black heart. So for the first time, we’re publishing a WIRED Yearbook: our very subjective, occasionally ridiculous, always enthusiastic collection of the people, institutions, inventions, and moments that offered optimism in 2026. I hope it gives you a healthy kick of bullishness—and the vigor to keep fighting for the future you want to see.
From the ecstatic night the Knicks won the NBA championship to the surprising ease with which New York absorbed the chaos of the World Cup to the record-low violent crime—it’s been a huge 2026 for the greatest city in the world. WIRED first sat down with Zohran Mamdani in 2025, when he was still just a candidate for mayor. A year later, as the midterm elections loomed, we returned.
KATIE DRUMMOND: We talked last year about social media as a tool for campaigning. How are you thinking about social media now as a tool for governance?
ZOHRAN MAMDANI: You have to continue to recognize the fact that for many New Yorkers, this is how they engage with the world. It is yet another medium that has to be treated with the same legitimacy and respect as traditional mediums.
What’s your point of view on the data center movement? Why do you think that specific issue has become such a flash point?
The movement to oppose data centers is one that gives me a real sense of hope.
It’s a bipartisan fight. What you’re seeing from Americans across the country is an opposition to what these data centers would mean for their day-to-day lives, what they would mean for their electricity rates, what they would mean for the environment. It’s also a repudiation of what has been governing politics for the last few years when it comes to AI, which is: Our risk, their reward.
Last year I asked you if technology was making democracy stronger or weaker. You said weaker. What about today?
I have family members sending me AI videos of me, thinking that they’re real. One complimented me on a 45-minute debate that I had with a European member of parliament. I was like, “This is not me.” There is a real crisis of faith as to what is real right now.
What do you hope the Democratic party looks like in, say, 2036?
I hope that party looks like one that realizes the only majority in this country is the working class, and fights for it. An ambitious version of the party cannot only be one that we find in history books. We need that to be a living, breathing politic. The people who run it have to be the American people.
In early August, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez announced that she was freezing her eggs . “Usually I keep my private life quite private,” she said in an Instagram video, before opening up about the process and sharing videos of the self-administered hormone injections.
This wasn’t an extraordinary event—more women than ever are making the same decision—but the internet exploded anyway. “This desire to start having children late in life is completely baffling to me,” wrote the far-right commentator Matt Walsh on X. “Totally backwards and ridiculous.”
Republicans weren’t all on the same page: Katie Miller, wife of the man recently promoted to White House chief of staff, defended AOC, writing on X, “If one woman wants to preserve her right to have children, which means more than having none—we should celebrate that.”
It is true that the Republican party has been intensely focused on women’s fertility . The expectation of motherhood, along with the proliferation of pro-natalism, has become core to the party. For conservative commentators to bash the New York representative felt incongruous at best. The White House itself reportedly didn’t love Walsh’s take.
Meanwhile, in an interview with ABC, Ocasio-Cortez said it was important to “normalize” the procedure at a time when “this administration is denying reproductive care to women across the country.”
As the 37-year-old congresswoman considers a presidential run in 2028, expect more of this. Conversations about her body, her health, and her possible maternal well-being will be front and center no matter what. She could have 100 children, and Republicans would spend time complaining about their names. —Leah Feiger
Australia restricted children’s access to social media at the end of 2025, and 2026 saw several other countries follow suit. Brazil banned features such as infinite scroll and autoplaying videos, also mandating more adult supervision and age checks. The European Union announced plans to prevent under-13s from using both social media and AI chatbots.
The jury’s still out on whether these bans actually work, but speaking of juries, let’s talk about Meta. After being accused of harming the brains of youngs everywhere, the company paid an $18 billion settlement, agreeing to new features like late-night restrictions and parental controls. “I’m proud of both the work Meta has done to protect kids historically and of this new groundbreaking agreement,” said the firm’s chief legal officer, lamely. If bans don’t work, lawsuits might. —Isabella Ward
Since October 2025, Bari Weiss, a longtime opinion journalist with no experience running a large organization, has been the editor in chief of CBS News. In that role, she has operated on a theory that has informed much of her career: People want common sense; her views (broadly, that the Israeli government is good and wokes are bad) are common sense; therefore, people want her views.
This worked fine when Weiss was editing The Free Press. At the time of that publication’s $150 million sale to Paramount last year, it had about 170,000 paid subscribers, a success by anyone’s estimation. Upon Weiss’ ascent at CBS News, a global operation with more than 1,000 employees, the question was whether Weiss’ skills were transferable.
It doesn’t look good. In January, Weiss tapped anchor Tony Dokoupil to take over CBS’s evening news broadcast; soon it was featuring Pete Hegseth interviews and even a “salute” to Marco Rubio. By April, the show was reportedly posting its lowest ratings ever.
Weiss persisted. She put Nick Bilton, a longtime opinion journalist with no experience running a large organization, in charge of 60 Minutes . The result? The show’s lowest ratings ever. Weiss, however, abides. —Tim Marchman
When people look back on 2026, they’ll likely remember Ms. Rachel for something unrelated to her kid-centric entertainment empire: offering an example, for adults, of how to be a good person.
Nothing says rock and roll like a marketing machine. Elvis had Colonel Tom Parker. The Rolling Stones had Andrew Loog Oldham. Geese has video clippers.
Social media users sensed something inorganic was happening on their For You pages after Geese released their album Getting Killed in September 2025. That and the band’s meteoric rise this year drove accusations that a “psyop” was afoot.
As WIRED wrote in April , the Brooklyn-based four-piece’s takeoff had indeed been somewhat staged: Digital marketing agency Chaotic Good Projects had been clipping and posting short videos of Geese content across a network of TikTok accounts to drive the band’s engagement. “It was low-effort TikTok posts that were used to boost the algorithm,” as frontman Cameron Winter put it to Rolling Stone. “They showed us samples, and it made me …

Clément Delangue, CEO of the open-source AI company Hugging Face , may go down in history as one of the first people ever attacked by a rogue AI agent. His company, which hosts millions of AI models and datasets, was breached in July when hundreds of agents being tested by OpenAI broke free from their sandbox and went on a hacking spree.
As the agents worked at superhuman speed to probe and exploit systems, Hugging Face confronted a bewildering deluge of data. The company’s engineers were only able to analyze the attack by using an open-weight model called GLM 5.2 from a Chinese company called Z.ai .
Delangue moved to the US more than a decade ago, “barely speaking English,” and built Hugging Face into a platform that supports tens of millions of AI developers. The fresh-faced Frenchman, who dresses even more like a skater than most AI execs, says the summer attack highlighted the value of open-weight models, which unlike ChatGPT or Claude can be downloaded and run by anyone.
Despite championing the democratization of AI, however, Hugging Face was acquired by one of the industry’s biggest players, Nvidia, for $12.93 billion in September. When I caught up with Delangue recently, that was the subject of my first question.
CLÉMENT DELANGUE: We need more resources to give open-source AI a chance. It has grown really well in the past few years and has become a really credible alternative to closed-source APIs. But the field is still dominated by closed-source.
We’re gonna have the Anthropic IPO in a few weeks. They basically went from zero to a top five or top 10 most valuable company in the world in a few years. I don't think that's ever happened before.
Does Anthropic's IPO suggest the closed approach is winning?
It’s hard to say. I've always said that there is a very strong natural tendency for AI to concentrate capabilities and wealth. People haven't internalized how much of the future compute capacity has already been reserved by a few companies. Talent, compute, resources—these all fuel the natural tendency for AI to be dominated by a few closed-source labs.
Let’s talk about the attack. When did you first realize Hugging Face was being hacked by a group of AI agents?
At the beginning, it didn't go to the top of our priority list. It just wasn't bad enough to really trigger that. The goal was pretty narrow and wasn’t deemed to be very dangerous or damaging. But it was raising questions. Especially the number of actions taken compared to the narrowness of the goal. It was surprising to us, and we couldn't really fit it into a familiar pattern. That's why we started investigating.
I actually think that 95 percent of the risks are being created by a few companies that are pushing the frontier behind closed doors. And 95 percent of the protection or defense is going to be done by the open-source ecosystem.
Does the US need its own open-weight models—ones as powerful as GLM, DeepSeek, Kimi, or Qwen ?
Yeah, I think it's very, very important for sovereignty, for understanding AI, and for academia. It’s kind of weird that most academic labs have to use Chinese models because they’re the ones that are open. If you go to Stanford or MIT, you have no choice but to use the Chinese open-weight models.
There is some momentum, but I don't think it's enough. I think there's a lot more to do. A lot more investment is needed.
The best open-source non-Chinese models are actually coming from outside of the US. Right from France, Mistral; Cohere from Canada; South Korea is starting to do more and more. But it’s still pretty far from what the US could do.
Perhaps we don’t need to panic about AI agents, but what about the idea of AI escaping human control due to recursive self-improvement?
You use a computer to write code. There's already some form of self-improvement in using the tools to build more tools. Now the question is how fast it accelerates. One thing that a lot of people realized this summer is that keeping AI behind closed doors in a few labs isn't actually safer. For recursive self-improvement, I think openness is a way to understand, follow, and regulate if we need to regulate.
Oh yeah, it's so fun, no? We're probably gonna sell over 50,000 of them this year. It's probably the most popular robot of the year.
We haven't talked about this much, but AI was really the unlock for the robot. We had the design for two years, but the problem was that when it fell, it couldn’t get up. And then at some point with reinforcement learning, one of our software engineers managed to get the Microduck to get itself back up.
At the end of the day, how do you convince people to take an interest in open-source AI?
Think of a world where two or three companies could write software and nobody else. That would be incredibly scary. It would mean that the whole world would be controlled by two or three companies. And unfortunately, that's kind of the direction that AI is taking right now.
Can open-source AI compete with something as capable as Claude or ChatGPT?
Yes, especially with agents. Many companies have shown that when you post-train your own model for your own use case, you get frontier—or even better than frontier—performance at a fraction of the cost.
I struggle a little bit with the meaning of that. Obviously the technology is progressing incredibly fast, and it’s more and more capable. I just don’t necessarily find it super useful to always compare AI to human capabilities. But if we’re getting to AGI or to superintelligence, it’s incredibly important that it’s as distributed as possible. The last thing you want is to have it concentrated in a few corporations.

“It’s definitely the largest art project I’ve ever worked on.”
Natalie Rosen is not the type of specialist you immediately associate with being one of the key people behind the new exhibit of the space shuttle Endeavour .
She is not a former NASA technician or engineer, as many of her colleagues have been for the past several years, nor is she a curator or conservator. Before this job, she had no experience working on any aircraft or spacecraft, as the new Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center, an extension of the California Science Center, opened in Los Angeles on November 13.
Without her expertise and artistry, however, the largest component of Endeavour ‘s “stack” would look nothing like it did when the shuttle was flying.
“My background is in the fine arts. I have my bachelor’s and my master’s in fine arts from Cal State Long Beach,” Rosen told collectSPACE.com . “When I came in on this project, they were looking for a sculptor, and I had been sculpting.”
Rosen had been working with mixed media for her thesis project and had experience sculpting foam. As it happened, the California Science Center had a lot of foam that needed shaping.
For those unfamiliar, the space shuttle was assembled from three primary launch components. The orbiter and its solid rocket boosters were reusable, given the time needed to inspect, service, and, in the case of the solid-fuel motors, refurbish and refill between flights.
The 154-foot-tall (47-meter) external tank was the only major part of the stack that was disposed of with each launch. After providing propellant for the orbiter’s three main engines, the tank was jettisoned and disintegrated while reentering the atmosphere.
To protect the orbiter from the extreme cold of the cryogenic liquid oxygen and liquid hydrogen in the external tank and to keep the propellant and oxidizer from boiling off too quickly, the ET was covered in insulating foam. (Some of that foam became liberated during ascent and was what caused the loss of the space shuttle Columbia and its crew in 2003.)
The only flight-worthy tank to remain at the end of the program was ET-94. A so-called lightweight tank, it was built at a time when NASA was transitioning to a super-lightweight model and was therefore set aside. Originally slated to support a science mission on Columbia, it instead became a testbed after the tragedy, having its foam stripped off and tested to better understand what had happened.
After the program ended, NASA donated ET-94 to the California Science Center. It arrived by way of a transoceanic barge and a road trip , then sat at Exposition Park for nearly a decade.
“So much of the foam on the ET had been dissected and removed during its time as a test article that they [the California Science Center] were trying to figure out how to put it back on and blend it in to the original foam in a convincing way,” said Rosen.
There has been a long-standing debate among shuttle enthusiasts and modelers about exactly what color the external tank is, and the answer resides in the foam.
“It’s orange. It’s cream. It’s burnt sienna. It just depends on the original foam, when you’re seeing it and how it’s aging. Because it starts as a kind of very ice cream white almost color, and then depending on how long it sits out in the Sun, it turns orange,” said Rosen.
By the time she had come on staff, the decision for the most part had already been made. Dennis Jenkins, the leader of the Endeavour project, had blended a special paint called “ET Orange” that was used to cover the existing acreage “bumpy” foam. Separately, a mocha-like color was picked out for the intertank.
“And then the latest foam to be installed, which would have looked the newest on all of the closeout hardware—the feed lines, the ice frost ramps, the flanges around the intertank and the intertank rings—those were all the lightest color that we custom mixed. That was what we called the ice cream color,” Rosen said.
It was not only about color matching, though. For multiple reasons, the original aerospace-grade foam could not be used, so a commercial substitute had to be found that could match what Rosen described as the “orange peel.”
“If you look at the tank very closely, there’s this bumpy texture, and there is a pattern from the original manufacturing and how it was sprayed on. There’s this overlapping line, a subtle-like stripe to it,” she said.
“There was a lot of trial and error in the beginning of what we could do to try and get it to match what was already there,” Rosen told collectSPACE. “We tried taking impressions off of the real foam and making molds and casting, but that didn’t really work. I then suggested we put in a dense urethane, like plain urethane foam, and I hand-sculpt the top of it to match what was around it. That ended up becoming the best solution for fixing the acreage foam that had an orange peel-like texture.”
Jenkins, who had worked as a space shuttle engineer and led NASA’s delivery of the orbiters to their museum homes, had high praise for Rosen and her work.
“She had to come up with a lot of new processes because we couldn’t apply foam the same way they did at Michoud. It’s not flightworthy by any means, but just coming up with how to make it look real took a lot of imagination on her part and she was pretty much a one-woman show for most of it,” he said.
Some of the repair work to the external tank was finished before it was lifted by crane into the Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center and mated with the boosters and Endeavour. From then on, Rosen had to climb scaffolding to get to her worksites.
“It’s definitely the largest art project I’ve ever worked on, and I mean I touched every inch of it,” Rosen said. “Once it went vertical, I was going up and down stairs. Probably the scariest was the point in the scaffolding where it just became ladders. So I had to be very, very careful and calculated in what I was doing.”
Even after the scaffolding was removed in preparation for the museum opening, Rosen’s ascents were not over. A couple of weeks ago, she had to install a final component on the aft dome of the liquid hydrogen tank. To reach that, she needed a scissor lift.
Now that the entire Endeavour stack has made its public debut , Rosen is not parting ways with the California Science Center. Her work on ET-94 has launched her career into a new frontier.
“In this last year, I have been working on different artifacts with the team. I have been helping leading up to the opening. I’ve helped in ways with the different aircraft, with their assembly, their disassembly, and reassembly. I’ve done some repairs in certain areas. I’ve worked with our satellite and probe collection to do repairs and also contacted specialists outside of my realm to clean and repair thermal blankets,” said Rosen.
“So I’m planning on staying with the museum for now. They’ve offered me another position, and I’m happy to stay,” she said.
The California Science Center’s Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center is now open to the public. Admission is free, but timed entry tickets are needed due to the high demand. Reservations can be made online or at 213-744-2019.

My wife and I were driving back from a date night. She was talking about a friend's very expensive utility bill, but I had missed the beginning of what she said (I was driving, after all).
Then I remembered: Wait, I can ask Siri to remind me! At a traffic light, I double-tapped the digital crown on the Apple Watch , and Siri's new Live Rewind feature spun back the clock 15 seconds and showed me a transcript of what my wife said.
I sheepishly interrupted her to show her the transcript. “Look!” Her reply? “Why wouldn't you just ask me to repeat myself?” She shrugged at this new Apple Watch capability and continued talking.
A few days later, I was chatting with my brother on my stoop. Once again, I lost focus for a few seconds and remembered to ask Siri to help me recall what my brother said moments ago. But this time, before I excitedly showed my brother the Apple Watch screen, I preemptively said, “Yeah, I know I could just ask you to repeat yourself.” I got a perplexed look back.
Live Rewind, one of Apple's new Audio Intelligence features on its latest Apple Watches, is designed to give you a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation. It's in public beta in watchOS 27.3, but is expected to launch officially before the year's end.
Coming alongside it is another new capability called Siri Recap: Give the assistant permission to listen to your environment—you can set schedules or have it trigger when you reach the office—and you'll see a “Recap” in the Siri app at the end of the day. It’ll show you summaries of conversations and list out important details that people said. It's very similar to AI notetakers , many of which run on dedicated hardware devices.
The power here is that it all happens on your Apple Watch, the same device you wear everywhere to track your fitness, monitor health, and check notifications. That ubiquity is exactly what makes privacy advocates uneasy—they say features like these normalize ambient surveillance , much like smart glasses , undermining the privacy of bystanders who don't consent to being recorded.
“One of the concerns that we have with things like the Apple Watch is we don't know what the watch is picking up on,” Reem Suleiman, senior campaign director at the nonprofit digital rights advocacy group Fight for the Future, tells WIRED. “Just because the device wearer is the one opting in to use the feature, you're not getting consent from everybody who you walk around.”
Apple has spent a great deal of effort explaining how the system works and how the company plans to maintain the privacy of its users and the people around them. First, these features are opt-in, and they are limited to the latest Apple Watch Series 12 or Apple Watch Ultra 4 . They also require an iPhone 16 or newer with iOS 27 and Apple Intelligence . These features are not available for users under 18, and they currently work only in English.
For Live Rewind, the audio is processed on-device and cannot be accessed. When you activate it, a small chime plays from the Apple Watch that serves as a warning for folks nearby. Text disappears unless you choose to save it to Siri. For Recaps, Siri keeps them factual, doesn't identify speakers, and also omits content the system deems sensitive. If you don't save a Recap, it'll self-delete in seven days. Apple uses its Private Cloud Compute processing system for the data, which is never stored or logged on its servers. Data stored in the Siri app is end-to-end encrypted when syncing with iCloud.
Siri Recaps are stored in the Siri app and will self-delete in seven days if you do not save them.
Even if you're happy with Apple's privacy focus, I haven't found these capabilities tremendously useful over the past week. Live Rewind works well in moderately quiet environments, but the transcript can quickly turn into inaccurate gibberish when there's a lot of background noise.
Activating it in front of the person you're chatting with feels awkward. It comes across like pulling out your smartphone when someone's trying to talk to you—a little rude and distracting. Instead of keeping screens out of sight—a big digital detox trend —you're introducing one in the middle of a human conversation. I brought the topic up with my wife again, and she echoed some of those feelings, saying it felt like a feature that would stunt a person's social skills. Instead of asking someone to repeat themself, they're bringing an Apple Watch into the mix to fill in the gaps.
I am not saying it can't be helpful. When it works, it feels like a superpower. Maybe there are certain situations where you don't want to interrupt a group conversation and ask someone to repeat themself. Right now, though, there's the problem of remembering that this feature exists and remembering to use it. I have also found the 15-second rule a little too short, and it resulted in me missing parts of the conversation.
Recap has been a little more helpful. For testing purposes, I've set Siri to capture recaps all day, every day, but I like that you can create a custom schedule or have it trigger when you arrive at a specific location, like the office. You can manually turn Siri Recap on or off in the Apple Watch's Control Center. Most impressive is that, despite having Recap enabled constantly, I haven't seen a meaningful dip in battery life. I've continued charging the Apple Watch Series 12 after a day and a half.
One of the more perplexing things was opening the Siri app to look at my recaps and finding a bunch of conversations I had no recollection of having. Turns out, Siri was recording media I was watching, like on YouTube or Instagram. This is a problem I encountered with AI notetakers, like the Amazon-owned Bee AI wearable , which claimed to be working on “liveness detection” to solve it. Its latest hardware shipped with a feature where it doesn't record a conversation if it doesn't detect the wearer's voice within a set period. Hopefully, Apple can figure out a solution. For now, you can edit or delete these recaps.
One day, I forgot to record an interview (though I took notes), and I knew the person said something that I hadn't written down. I headed over to Siri and found exactly what I was looking for—paraphrased, but there. That said, the Recaps aren't designed to be detailed summaries and action plans from your meetings or conversations, unlike dedicated AI notetakers. They're meant to jog your memory. At times, I wish Siri were more detailed, but if that's what you're after, you'll have to invest in a third-party device.
Recap can be helpful for work meetings, but I haven't personally found it all that compelling in my personal life. Looking back at what it has picked up over conversations with friends and family, the only thing I feel is: Yep, those conversations happened . A friend was talking about their woodworking hobby—they can't use oil-based polyurethane as a finish in the winter months as it stays tacky. Siri logged this in such a matter-of-fact way, but when I revisited the conversation in the recap, I didn't find it helpful, useful, or interesting. (No offense, friend!) It's just nuggets of life.
Apple has pulled off impressive feats with these features, capturing these moments in a way that feels a little more privacy-preserving than competitors, without tanking the already limited battery life of its smartwatches. But socially, we're still figuring out what it means to walk around with always-on passive recorders. For now, I'm happy to stick with my wife's advice and ask: “Come again?”

Astronauts have a well-deserved reputation for being focused on their work. After spending years preparing for a single mission, they’re all business as they hurtle through the cosmos, ever vigilant that a brief lapse in concentration can mean catastrophe. That mindset is a big reason why the crew of NASA ’s Artemis II was so oblivious to their celebrity as they circumnavigated the moon in April. It wasn’t until the seventh day of their nearly 10-day journey that they began to realize their exploits were causing a massive stir back home.
“We were talking to our families for the second time,” recalls Jeremy Hansen, the sole Canadian in the four-person crew. “And that’s when we all heard, one after another: ‘Hey, this is really resonating on the planet in a way that you’re going to be shocked by.’”
Hansen and his comrades were overwhelmed by their fame once they splashed back down on Earth. Nearly 150 million people had watched the mission’s key moments on NASA’s online platforms, which included feeds with near-constant access to the interior of the Orion spacecraft. The buzz around the mission harkened back to the glory days of American spaceflight, when people would gather around TV sets to marvel at astronauts floating outside their capsules or bounding around the moon.
The romantic spirit of the Artemis program’s long-term objective certainly helped: People are alive to the dream of a moon base that’s meant to serve our species’ idealistic aspirations rather than be a zillionaire’s private plaything. Artemis II supported that noble mission by putting the Orion ’s life-support, navigation, and piloting systems through their paces. But fans were also drawn to the crew’s infectious energy. There was palpable chemistry between Hansen, Christina Koch, Victor Glover, and Reid Wiseman, all of whom exuded pure joy and wonder as they dealt with the minutiae of life aboard a multibillion-dollar vehicle traveling as fast as 25,000 miles per hour.
“It was not a natural thing for us,” admits Hansen. “You have four type-A personalities who are willing to strap themselves to a rocket and go to the moon. We were doing stuff for the first time, and it was not uncommon for us to have four different opinions.” When the astronauts began to notice that interpersonal friction was becoming problematic during training, they enlisted the aid of professionals. During a September 2024 training trip to Iceland, the crew spent two extra days in conversations and teamwork exercises organized by Rick Rochelle, a renowned leadership guru. Once the Artemis II schedule was firmed up, the crew made a pact: Launch as friends, land as friends.
Their historic flight past the far side of the moon marked the apex of that friendship. They were more than 250,000 miles away from Earth. The planet looked no bigger than a fingernail sliver—“just this lifeboat hanging undisturbingly in the universe,” Koch would later say during the crew’s first public remarks after touchdown. “You look at it, and you just kind of shake your head,” says Hansen. “How can we do anything other than lift one another up and try to make life better for one another?”
Then that “tiny Earth” vanished as the spacecraft went behind the moon, and the crew spent 40 minutes out of radio contact. They carved out a few seconds to toast each other with maple cookies—carefully, to keep crumbs from floating free in zero gravity. They also selected a crater to name for Wiseman’s late wife, Carroll, who died of cancer in 2020. Soon after they reemerged from total isolation, they came together in an ecstatic, four-person embrace. “I knew right there that we were going to be bound together for life,” Wiseman says.
There were plenty of lowlights during the mission, too. Some lint got trapped in the primary urine vent line, Wiseman says, “so we had to go to a backup method of urination, which for the men wasn’t bad, but for the woman wasn’t great.” Another hiccup involved a smoke detector that erroneously went off while the spacecraft was still 80,000 miles from home, leading to 15 minutes of intense anxiety.
None of the Artemis II crew members are likely to return to space: Hansen, Glover, and Wiseman have all moved on from astronaut life, and Koch transitioned into a leadership role at NASA. Their new, less stressful lives should give them ample opportunity to cheer on Artemis III, tentatively scheduled to launch in summer 2027—an event that may once again remind us that we’re all part of a shared story far bigger than ourselves.
What did we miss? Tell us about your favorite moments of 2026 in the comments below.

When Silicon Valley entrepreneur Chad Steelberg decided he wanted to get involved in the war in Ukraine, he had no idea where to start. So the then CEO of enterprise AI company Veritone did what he knew best: built an artificial intelligence model to help him figure it out. Today, he has proprietary munition and missile designs, several government partnerships, and a defense-as-a-service business valued at more than $1 billion.
Steelberg, alongside fellow Google alumnus and former Apple executive Andy Baynes, says they are trying to break the Russia-Ukraine war “stalemate,” Silicon Valley–style. They believe their experience building and iterating technology quickly can help bring Western weapon manufacturing in line with the rapid innovation cycles seen on the battlefield and beat the “attritional cat-and-mouse technology game” that the war, as Baynes describes it, has become.
Steelberg, originally from Newport Beach, California, started itching to “make a difference” on the battlefield after he took in a couple hundred Ukrainian refugees into his French chateau in early 2022. He says he was regularly “heartbroken” by the outpouring of grief whenever bad news arrived about a husband, father, or son back home. “I believe I could really change the outcome of this and every war,” Steelberg tells WIRED. "I'm not saying this is purely altruistic,” he adds. “Of course we're going to be making money doing it."
This week, their firm, Tiberius Aerospace, said it had secured $85 million in Series A financing, led by European technology investment firm Lakestar and Rochefort Asset Management, a national-security-focused investment firm licensed under the US Defense Department. Ukrainian venture capital firm UA1 is also an investor.
Tiberius began as Steelberg’s private research lab, incorporated in 2021, which employed people across France, the UK, and US to experiment on left-field ideas across a range of technologies, from drones and electric vertical takeoff aircraft to quantum computing. After the invasion, he pivoted the lab’s AI and aerospace engineers into writing code and building spreadsheets to objectively analyze the war’s many factors and calculate what could move the needle. The AI model they created quickly ruled out building better defensive technology because that would just harden the stalemate.
With his aim narrowed to building an offensive weapon, Steelberg developed several metrics to numerically analyze the lethality of different systems, including cost-effectiveness, and used the AI engine to simulate weapons under different conditions and identify what would disrupt the market. Don’t build another drone, it suggested, build longer-range artillery munitions. The resulting system, called Sceptre, can be fired from a 155-millimeter howitzer—the most common artillery weapon donated to Ukraine. As well as traveling farther than currently available rounds, they claim they can reach supersonic speeds and altitudes beyond jamming range.
Giving Ukraine’s guns extra range is important, Sam Cranny-Evans, an associate fellow at UK defense think tank the Royal United Services Institute, tells WIRED, because it would allow Ukrainian gunners to operate beyond the reach of Russian drone attacks. 155-mm shells “can cause massive damage to a group of vehicles or infantry,” he says. “Any technology that can help Ukraine extend the reach of its howitzers and return them to combat would be valuable.”
With a prototype he’d designed with the help of AI, Steelberg also started to expand the Tiberius team, including bringing on board Baynes as chief strategy officer in 2023. Baynes had first traveled to Ukraine around a decade ago to investigate how local startup Ring , now owned by Amazon, had outdone Nest , which he’d been working on and eventually sold to Google. He fell in love with Kyiv’s ambitious software engineers and booming tech scene–responsible for globally successful tech tools like Grammarly and Snapchat’s face filters. In 2016, he bought a local life-science tech company with the aim of accelerating next-generation medicines through automating clinical trials and improving protein modeling. “What drew me into Kyiv was the hunger and ambition in the engineering community,” he tells WIRED. “It was difficult to not be enormously attracted to that and to see if it's something that could be put into really critical-mission problem sets like cancer drugs or speeding up clinical trials for life-science companies.”
After the Russian invasion, Baynes set himself up in Budapest for around six months to help with the logistics of evacuating women and children and moving equipment into the country. He asked his global network for help finding medical equipment, vehicles, and accommodation for refugees—bringing him back in touch with Steelberg. Baynes believes the West’s response to the invasion has been “inadequate” and that Ukraine needs better offensive capabilities to push Russia’s army back.
In April, Tiberius announced it had successfully fired one of its Sceptre projectiles from a NATO-standard 155-mm howitzer for the first time. It is now working with the US Army to mature the system, and it has announced a $500 million technology collaboration contract with UK partners to manufacture, license, and distribute the munition. It is also developing a missile, which it expects to start generating revenue next year.
Tiberius has turned the AI system it initially built into a product called GRAIL (Generative Real-Time Artificial Intelligence for Lethality). Steelberg says he is “most excited about” this. He hopes the platform can enable continuous upgrades to the weapon designs Tiberius licenses by decentralizing manufacturing. Steelberg says that, as well as automating supply chain management and compliance, the software simulates weapons against different targets in a range of environments and weather conditions, such as an Arctic peninsula. In addition to open-sourced data, the team is trying to get hold of much sought-after active combat data from around the world, including Ukraine. The idea is that this all enables users to test, iterate, and design weapons for specific uses much quicker.
“In the world of AI and design and development getting faster and faster, what is it that the West or the group of allied nations have an undeniable advantage on?” Baynes asks. “If you can weaponize all of the spare capacity and precision manufacturing across the UK, France, Germany, the Nordic countries, the US,” he says, “that's something that our adversaries today can never ever match.” Tiberius aims to achieve this by copying “the Apple model,” continues Baynes, who reported to Steve Jobs for four years. He says outsourcing manufacturing to many third-party subcontractors can accelerate development and deployment and keeps expensive production costs off Tiberius’ balance sheet during peacetime.
“We're taking the approach of Silicon Valley,” says Steelberg. “When you run into a big, hard, hairy problem, you not only cross that, but you turn around, you build a bridge—it’s a toll bridge, obviously—so the entire industry can cross that hurdle faster, better, stronger. They might pay a small fee, but it's better than dying in the ditch and not making it across it.”
