Ukrainian officials have accused Russia of targeting rescue and recovery operations two weeks after a deadly "double-tap" strike at a village close to the front line killed at least 72 people.
Ukraine says Russia carried out two attacks in succession on a humanitarian aid centre in the village of Komyshuvakha on 2 November - including the use of what it said was a 3,000kg (6,600lb) aerial bomb on a shelter where residents had fled for safety.
Verified images posted in the days after the attack show damage to emergency vehicles and excavation equipment at the site.
The State Emergency Service of Ukraine (DSNS) told BBC Verify there were multiple Russian strikes during the rescue.
The DSNS said three police officers, four workers and two rescue dogs were injured while five vehicles were damaged during the operation, which has now concluded.
With the DSNS saying the death toll had risen to at least 72 people, the attack on Komyshuvakha has become the second deadliest single incident of the Ukraine war.
Oleksiy, an intelligence officer investigating the incident for Ukraine's SBU security service, who asked to be identified only by his first name, said rescue vehicles were "clearly marked" and accused Russia of "deliberately destroying humanitarian equipment".
He added the village's infrastructure and the people still living in Komyshuvakha are also being systematically targeted by drones and bombs. Oleksiy accused Russian forces of "outright terror against civilians, against peaceful residents" to make life on the front line impossible.
BBC Verify has confirmed videos being shared by Ukrainian police that show rescue workers at the scene shouting "drone, drone" and running for cover on the day after the 2 November attack. A group can also be seen treating a victim.
Oleksiy said rescue crews operated under a constant threat of attack. "The enemy knows perfectly well that what is being carried out there is essentially a humanitarian operation to search for the dead," he said.
BBC Verify has asked the Russian Ministry of Defence for comment specifically about the Komyshuvakha attacks but has not received a response.
A general statement released on 2 November by the Russian MoD said it had targeted energy and transport infrastructure used by the Ukrainian military across the country.
While there are no military or industrial facilities in Komyshuvakha it is close to a key route used for Ukrainian troop movements, supplies and evacuations. The village was previously reported to have been struck by the Russians on 28 October.
Local people headed to the shelter area on 2 November after being told by a local Telegram group that aid would be distributed between 10:00 and 12:00 local time (08:00-10:00 GMT). Ukrainian authorities said an initial strike, at 09:45 local time, hit buildings above ground killing one woman.
Video shows moments between deadly Russian attacks on village in Ukraine
Bodycam footage, released by Ukrainian police in edited segments and analysed by BBC Verify, shows people trying to free a casualty from the rubble before declaring she had died.
Throughout the footage, warnings of an impending second strike can be heard on police radios with increasing urgency until people are instructed to run to the underground shelter.
The same footage, which was taken around an hour after the first attack, goes on to show people in a shelter. As they wait in silence a large explosion can be heard and the video goes dark.
Aftermath video filmed later shows bodies being recovered from a large crater immediately above the shelter. Twisted iron and rubble from the structure below can be seen beneath the surface.
Funerals have been held almost daily for the victims of the attack, including locals working to administer aid distribution, those seeking to collect it and soldiers who officials say arrived to assist with rescue efforts.
Trevor Ball, bomb disposal expert at intelligence firm at Armament Research Services, said a crater seen in the footage was consistent with the damage and depth left by a FAB-3000, a 3,000kg Russian bomb which can destroy underground structures.
His comments were echoed by Chris Proops, an ex-UK National Crime Agency investigator, who said the scale of the damage at the scene matched the size of the FAB-3000.
Ball and Proops both confirmed verified photos of munition fragments obtained by BBC Verify from Ukrainian authorities show part of a guidance kit that is compatible with the FAB-3000, which increases the weapon's accuracy and allows it to be fired from a greater distance from the target.
International law experts told BBC Verify that Russia had committed a war crime if it knowingly attacked rescue workers.
Ben Saul, professor of international law at the University of Sydney, said this "appears to be either a deliberate attack on civilians or civilian objects - a war crime - or an indiscriminate attack - also a war crime".
Prof Samuel Moyn of Yale University said "directly targeting rescuers or their equipment is a gross violation of international humanitarian law". Precautions have to be taken to ensure that strikes target combatants rather than others, he added.

There is always a catch. Or in the case of Tesla ’s self-driving Cybercab , several.
Last Friday night, Tesla said it had invited “select customers” to purchase their very own Cybercabs. The two-seat, gold vehicle is unlike any other on the market: It lacks a steering wheel and brake pedals, and is primarily driven by software. (Other autonomous vehicle companies, including Alphabet's Waymo and Amazon’s Zoox , offer self-driving rides on ride-hail networks , but don’t let people buy their cars.) Tesla’s " limited release ” will supposedly offer some people (unclear how many) the opportunity to pay $29,900 to take delivery in December.
From there, though, the Cybercab will need constant cash infusions to stay on the road.
The business model raises questions about what people will actually get when they buy a Cybercab. “You’ll never really own the car,” says Ivan Drury, the director of insights at Edmunds. “It’s more like $30,000 to buy into a franchise.”
According to documents posted on Tesla’s website, the vehicle “will not operate” without what Tesla is calling an “autonomy subscription," a monthly fee that will start at $299. If owners don’t pay on time and in full, their self-driving cars won’t work. If they try to operate the vehicles in areas that don’t support the service—right now, they’re restricted to portions of cities in Florida and Texas—their self-driving cars won’t work. (That area can expand, contract, or “relocate” at any time.)
If owners do anything that Tesla deems "unauthorized or inappropriate," the company says it can suspend or cancel the subscription—and their self-driving cars won’t work. If the vehicle loses connectivity, the self-driving cars won’t work. (“Tesla is not responsible for carrier, spectrum, environmental, or other external outages,” its “autonomy agreement” says.)
Tesla also reserves the right to make an owner’s car not work at any time: It says it can, for any safety or security purpose, suspend or terminate access to Cybercab tech, or restrict operations by location, road type, weather, or “condition.” This is particularly salient because the Cybercab is also under investigation by US safety regulators , who are trying to understand why Tesla believes the vehicle meets safety standards without so many of the parts and systems required.
For years, automakers have seen increasingly software-dominated vehicles as an opportunity to get drivers hooked on the same special sauce that makes Netflix, Amazon, and Spotify so potent: monthly subscription services . Because these vehicles can receive over-the-air software updates, manufacturers can offer drivers new services as they make them. The upside is high, tech-style margins that keep rolling in, versus the razor-thin ones seen in car-making. A 2024 report suggested that connected-car features could one day be a $200 billion industry.
In some ways, the subscription model is working. Today, some automakers charge extra for remote start, security, internet connectivity, and advanced driver assistance features. General Motors said it made $2.7 billion in subscription-related revenue last year from fees drivers paid for its OnStar and Super Cruise services.
But some customers have also found the business model yucky, or even offensive. Why charge extra to “unlock” a feature that’s already built into a car? If an automaker can add a new feature at any time, can’t they also take it away? And if they can take it away, what does "ownership" mean? In 2022, BMW told drivers in select countries it would activate factory-installed heated seats for a monthly or one-time fee ; it eventually backed down after public outcry, pledging the company would no longer charge subscription fees for pre-installed hardware. (BMW is still pursuing a subscription model for some features.) “Consumers hate being nickel-and-dimed for subscriptions,” says Drury.
Tesla was an early mover in the subscription feature space and has offered connectivity and driver-assistance features for monthly or one-time fees for a decade. As the company has shifted away from making cars and toward robotics and autonomous vehicles , executives have made clear that charging for services is the future. (Its Robotaxi service currently picks up fare-paying passengers in parts of eight US cities.) So Tesla buyers may be particularly amenable to paying monthly to make their self-driving cars go.
In exchange for monthly fees, buyers will also get access to other services, too, including remote support , roadside assistance, tire, air filter, and windshield wiper replacements, and tire and camera inspections. (The agreement says that list might change, too.) Cybercabs will be able to “travel autonomously, unoccupied to a Tesla service center,” the company says. The fee doesn't cover insurance.
Cybercab buyers will have other restrictions. The vehicle is for personal use only. Even though CEO Elon Musk has repeatedly said owners will be able to put their vehicles on Tesla’s wider Robotaxi network to make money during downtime, and even has an online interest form for those who want to own and operate their own Cybercab fleets, the current ownership agreement prohibits that. Buyers are also prohibited from selling or transferring their vehicles without Tesla’s written consent. The company “advises against” children under 13 riding in the Cybercab, and prohibits children from riding without an adult present.
In a post on X , Musk showed no apparent compunction about the Cybercab business model, but did say the monthly price for autonomy “is too high.” He wrote that the price should be “more like ~$115/month.”

Moscow-installed governor says traffic suspended after second attack on bridge in two days.
A Ukrainian drone attack has killed at least two people in Russian-annexed Crimea as Kyiv has targeted the only bridge connecting southern Russia to the Black Sea peninsula for the second consecutive day, according to the Moscow-installed governor.
In a Telegram post, Sergei Aksyonov said traffic has been suspended after Tuesday’s attack on the Kerch Bridge .
Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed the “unprecedented” attack, publishing footage on social media on Tuesday that showed the main arch of the bridge for cars and part of its roadway collapsed.
He said the targeting came in response to Russian strikes on Ukraine’s infrastructure.
The bridge in the Kerch Strait, which connects the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov, stretches for 19km (11.8 miles) and is also used by trains.
Reporting from Moscow, Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova said Russia came under one of the largest Ukrainian drone attacks on Monday night.
“According to official data from the Ministry of Defence, Russian air defence systems destroyed more than 1,400 drones over 23 regions, including border regions and regions in central Russia. Meanwhile, the mayor of Moscow said that more than 800 drones flew towards the capital,” Shapovalova reported.
Also on Tuesday, Moscow attacked two bridges in Kyiv, Russia’s Ministry of Defence said.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said in a Telegram post that ⁠the Northern and ⁠Southern bridges had been hit and the subway ⁠system ⁠had also been damaged. He added that water and power supplies had been ‌partially cut.
The Russian Defence Ministry said it also targeted Ukraine’s military infrastructure in attacks on Monday night, including facilities used to produce cruise missiles and long‑ and medium‑range drones. The ministry said transport and energy facilities were also targeted as well as port infrastructure and ships used by the Ukrainian military.
Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine said the first of a “series of very loud explosions” rang out in Kyiv just before midnight.
“Another round of explosions was heard just after 5am [03:00 GMT] this morning,” she said.
“Some bridges were damaged. We understand that they are still standing, but there is no traffic on either of them. These are bridges that are used every day by civilians to commute around the city. These attacks also cut heating to hundreds of apartment buildings on Kyiv’s Left Bank.”
The exchange of attacks comes just days before a meeting of Presidents Vladimir Putin of Russia, Xi Jinping of China and Donald Trump of the United States in China’s Shenzhen region.
The Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs said Thursday’s talks will focus on topics of “groundbreaking significance”, including “safeguarding world peace”.
Trump has made securing an end to the war between Russia and Ukraine a key part of his presidency. Despite another round of talks held in the United Arab Emirates last week, US mediators have failed to make a breakthrough.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had warned that Kyiv would carry out attacks on Russia in the days before the meeting.

Zelenskyy praises ‘unprecedented attack’ but Kremlin claims bridge will be restored and will be ‘better than ever’
Ukraine has critically damaged the Kerch bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia in an overnight missile attack, in what Volodymyr Zelenskyy hailed as an “unprecedented” military operation.
Footage showed a Ukrainian Flamingo cruise missile seconds before it hit the road and railway crossing, followed by an explosion. The strike follows an earlier attack on Monday that targeted an arch across its central section.
Writing on social media, the Ukrainian president described the attack as “a response to Russian strikes on our infrastructure”. He said it was the culmination of a long and complex campaign to demolish the bridge, involving domestically produced drones and ballistic missiles.
“Our warriors gradually destroyed air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective,” he wrote. Palianytsia drones hit the road section of the bridge, while Neptune and other missiles targeted the adjacent rail section, he added.
Earlier, Russian forces struck ⁠two major bridges in Kyiv that straddle the Dnipro River late on Monday, along with some other critical infrastructure, amid drone ⁠and missile attacks ​across Ukraine.
Ukraine has declared that the Kerch bridge, built eight years ago after Vladimir Putin’s 2014 annexation of Crimea and known officially as the Crimean Bridge, is illegal. It has repeatedly attempted to destroy it, using a truck bomb in 2022 and a sea drone strike the following year.
The latest drone and missile barrage appears to have succeeded after months in which Ukrainian unmanned systems forces have systematically knocked out the peninsula’s multi-layered air defences.
The Kremlin-appointed governor of Crimea, Sergey Aksyonov, confirmed that the bridge, which was temporarily closed on Monday, was no longer usable. “The enemy has once again attacked the Crimean Bridge. At the moment, traffic has been suspended,” he posted on Telegram.
He added: “We ask residents and visitors in Crimea to refrain from travelling toward the bridge and to take these restrictions into account when planning their routes.”
Photos on Tuesday suggest that a 227-metre road arch span has fallen into the Kerch strait, which connects the Sea of Azov with the Black Sea. The adjacent railway arch span has also sustained damage.
Ukrainian commentators say the massive steel arch cannot easily be replaced. The closure of the bridge means traffic from Crimea can travel out of the peninsula only via a land corridor through occupied southern Ukraine, vulnerable to Ukrainian drones.
The debris appears to have blocked the main navigable route beneath the bridge, used by maritime traffic from the Sea of Azov and the ports of Berdiansk and Mariupol. The channel is 120 metres wide and 8.3 metres deep. Submerged steel struts could prevent large vessels from passing until the debris is removed.
The Russian government convened an emergency meeting to assess the attack, after which one of the country’s deputy prime ministers, Marat Khusnullin, briefed Putin on the damage to the bridge, according to the Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov.
Peskov added that the bridge would be repaired and would be “even better than before”, in comments to the Russian newspaper Izvestia.
But pro-war Russian commentators acknowledged that repairing the bridge would be very difficult, warning that, unlike in 2022 and 2023, Ukraine now had the capability to strike floating cranes and repair crews.
“Even installing a prefabricated arch under such conditions would be a formidable challenge,” wrote the influential Rybar Telegram channel, with close links to the defence ministry.
Ukrainian observers were gleeful at the bridge’s long-awaited destruction. They also pointed out that Ukraine’s armed forces could hit the bridge again to prevent repair work from being carried out. Serhii Sternenko, a former adviser to the defence ministry in Kyiv, wrote: “In response to your many questions. Yes, the bridge is fucked.”
The Ukrainian blogger Anton Gerashchenko pointed out that Putin personally opened the bridge in 2018, driving across it in a Kamaz truck. “The Kerch bridge stands as the primary symbol of the Russian occupation of Ukrainian Crimea and the embodiment of its illegal annexation. It is Putin’s flagship project,” he wrote.
He added: “For years, Russian authorities claimed the bridge was ‘the most protected facility in the world’. Consequently, every successful strike shatters the myth of the invincibility of Russian air defences – as well as the notion that Ukraine is incapable of reaching key targets deep behind enemy lines.”
Ukrainians celebrated on Tuesday with memes. The company Fire Point, which manufactures the Flamingo missile, posted a popcorn emoji. Other social media users shared video of “Kerch Bridge on Fire” , a popular song by Saint Javelin which has become an anti-Moscow anthem.
Russian military bloggers were gloomy. One, Russian Engineer, acknowledged the Ukrainian military operation to paralyse the bridge had been “perfect”. Hundreds of unmanned aerial vehicles distracted Russian air defences, he said, before a clinical strike by ballistic missiles.
The attack will further complicate supplies to Crimea, after a summer in which the peninsula struggled with fuel shortages and an intensifying Ukrainian campaign to isolate it from mainland Russia.
Ukraine has for months focused its strikes on the key transport routes supplying Crimea, particularly the so-called Novorossiya highway, a key logistics corridor linking the peninsula to Russia’s Rostov region through the occupied cities of Melitopol and Mariupol.
Russia had already sharply restricted traffic across the Crimean bridge. Moscow has largely stopped using the crossing for rail fuel shipments since the 2022 Ukrainian attack damaged the bridge and set a fuel train ablaze.
Rybar wrote that the latest strike would force Moscow to “completely overhaul” its supply routes to Crimea, shifting more traffic to the Novorossiya highway.
Russia would also have to step up the installation of protective netting along the route, Rybar added, lamenting that the measure had not been introduced in the spring.
Meanwhile in Kyiv, loud explosions could be heard as Russian forces struck two bridges over the Dnipro River. The mayor of the Ukrainian capital, Vitali Klitschko, wrote on Telegram that according to “preliminary information, there have been hits on the north and south bridges in ⁠the capital”. There were water and power cuts in parts of the city, he added later.
Russian forces launched a ​series of attacks on bridges crossing ‌the river earlier this ‌month and in October.
A Russian missile attack injured three people ‌in the region of Cherkasy and also targeted Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second biggest city, local officials said on Telegram.
Russia’s defence ministry claimed ⁠on ⁠Tuesday its ​forces had ⁠carried out a massive ⁠overnight strike ​on ‌Ukrainian ‌military-industrial facilities, ‌transport infrastructure in Kyiv and Zaporizhzhia and the ‌Cherkasy and Dnipropetrovsk regions.
The ministry ​said the strikes also ⁠targeted energy facilities, ​port infrastructure ​and ​vessels ​used ‌by ​Ukraine’s armed ​forces.
The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said earlier on Monday that intelligence showed Russia’s military was planning strikes for Monday evening and throughout Tuesday.
Russian defence ministry data from Monday showed that an overnight Ukrainian drone barrage was the biggest since the start of full-scale war in 2022.
Zelenskyy also said on Monday ⁠that Ukraine had held new online talks with the US presidential envoys ​Steve Witkoff and ​Jared Kushner, as well as European ​representatives, on the prospects of ending the war with Russia.

Ukraine has severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, in what Volodymyr Zelensky says was an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.
Images shared by Ukrainian officials show a section of the Crimean Bridge - also known as the Kerch Bridge - has collapsed into the water, dealing a logistical and symbolic blow to Russia's war effort.
A Kremlin spokesperson insisted the bridge would be rebuilt "better than before".
Elsewhere, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the Northern and Southern bridges, both important crossings over the Dnipro River, were closed after Russia targeted the Ukrainian capital overnight.
Ukraine has long targeted the Crimean Bridge, which provides a road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line, but has struggled to close it for good.
The damage reported on Tuesday appeared to be far more severe than previously, with a large arched section of the bridge apparently destroyed.
Video footage appeared to show critical damage to the road section, with remnants of the support arch and road deck seen protruding from the water below.
Zelensky said the overnight strike was the result of a seven-stage operation by the military and security services, which saw Ukrainian forces "gradually destroy air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective".
He said the rail section parallel to the bridge's road had also been hit by a wave of drones, though images showed its supporting arch was still standing and a Russian-backed official said some rail services were operating.
The bridge was built by Russia after it invaded and annexed the peninsula in 2014, and was personally opened by Russian President Vladimir Putin in 2018.
While Ukraine has been trying to increase the cost to Russia of waging war economically, by hitting oil refineries and depots, striking the bridge is an attempt to increase the political cost on Putin.
The timing of the strike comes at a significant moment, ahead of Putin meeting the leaders of China and the US. This could cloud his moment back in the spotlight.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge would "be restored following Ukrainian strikes, and it will be even better than before", and did not rule out the possibility the strikes were linked to Putin's visit to China.
Russia's Investigative Committee confirmed structural damage and said it had opened a "criminal case... on terrorism charges" after attacks by "Ukraine's armed formations".
For the second day in a row, Russia recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, with 2,256 drones downed, according to the defence ministry.
There was heavy traffic in Kyiv on Tuesday after two major crossings were closed after strikes
Zelensky had warned of major attacks in the days leading up to a meeting between Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in China's Shenzhen on Thursday.
Loud explosions were heard in Kyiv just before midnight on Tuesday, with Klitschko saying shortly after that the city had suffered "damage to critical infrastructure systems" and disruption to heating and water.
Some of Kyiv's above-ground subway services were damaged in the overnight attacks, officials said, after civilians were told to go to civil defence shelters.
Eight major bridges span the Dnipro River connecting the western and eastern parts of Kyiv, and an estimated three million residents rely on the bridges to travel across the city.
Strikes on the busy Northern and Southern Bridges will cause major disruption to people's daily lives.
Elsewhere, three people have been injured in a Russian missile attack in the Cherkasy region, according to local officials.
The long-term impact of the Crimean Bridge strike is still not fully clear though the risk of a serious transport and logistics crisis for the Russian military has increased significantly.
The collapse of the arched section of the Crimean Bridge has cut off the peninsula's direct road and rail links with Russia – at least until the crossing can be repaired.
However, there is still a land corridor running through the occupied parts of the Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions - though Ukraine has been systematically striking transport routes across northern Crimea, as well as bridges and other crossings in the area around Chongar.
This has already caused problems with the delivery of fuel and other supplies, including military cargo.
There is a ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait. It could partly compensate for the loss of the bridge, but its capacity is very limited and it is also vulnerable to attack.
Russia could also supply Crimea by sea, but this route is also risky, as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones operate extensively in the area.
In addition, debris from the Crimean Bridge – particularly its enormous arch – may have blocked the shipping channel.
This would make it harder for larger vessels to pass through and create further problems for ports in the Sea of Azov, including Mariupol and Berdiansk.
Russia's launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control.

Meta , Instagram'ın mesajlaşma deneyimini ayrı bir uygulamaya taşıyan Direct isimli yeni uygulamasını test etmeye başladı. Şimdilik yalnızca Türkiye ve Tayland'da kullanıma sunulan Direct, kullanıcıların Instagram hesabına sahip olmadan da mesajlaşabilmesine imkan tanıyor.
Direct'in arayüzü, Instagram'ın mevcut mesaj kutusuna oldukça benziyor. Instagram hesabıyla giriş yapan kullanıcıların mevcut sohbetleri yeni uygulamaya aktarılıyor. Uygulamada sohbetlere özel arka planlar oluşturma ve Instagram'ın kısa durum güncellemeleri sunan Notlar özelliği de bulunuyor.
Direct'i kullanmak için Instagram hesabına sahip olmanız gerekmiyor. Kullanıcılar e-posta adresleri veya telefon numaralarıyla yeni bir Direct hesabı oluşturabiliyor. Ancak Instagram hesabı olmadan uygulamayı kullananların, sohbet başlatmak istedikleri kişileri Instagram kullanıcı adı veya QR kod aracılığıyla manuel olarak eklemesi gerekiyor.
Meta, Instagram'daki bazı güvenlik özelliklerini Direct'e de taşıyor. Buna göre kullanıcılar, bağlantı kurmadıkları kişilerle doğrudan sohbet başlatamıyor. Şirket ayrıca genç kullanıcılarla gerçekleştirilebilecek uygunsuz etkileşimleri tespit etmek ve bunlara müdahale etmek için teknolojiden yararlanacağını belirtiyor. Ancak bu sistemin nasıl çalışacağına ilişkin ayrıntılar henüz resmi olarak paylaşılmadı. Meta'nın ebeveyn denetimi araçlarını kullanan aileler ise gençlerin Direct üzerinden kimlerle mesajlaştığını ve uygulamada ne kadar zaman geçirdiğini takip edebilecek.
Direct'in ortaya çıkışı, Instagram'ın son yıllarda giderek daha fazla mesajlaşma odaklı bir platforma dönüşmesi açısından da dikkat çekici. Instagram'ın 2017'nin Aralık ayında mesajlaşma özelliğini Direct adı altında ayrı bir uygulama olarak yayınladığını hatırlatalım . Şirket, 2019 yılında Direct uygulamasını kapatma kararı almıştı. 2020 yılında ise Instagram Threads, Direct'in yerini almaya hazırlanmaktaydı .
Öte yandan Instagram Başkanı Adam Mosseri , daha önce mesajlaşmanın Instagram'da en fazla kullanılan özelliklerden biri olduğunu birçok kez dile getirmişti. Buna karşın Mosseri, geçmişte Instagram mesaj kutusunun Threads'e taşınması fikrine mesafeli yaklaşmış ve aynı kişilere birden fazla uygulama üzerinden ulaşmanın gereksiz bir deneyim yaratabileceğini belirtmişti.
Meta'nın şimdi Instagram mesajlaşmasını tamamen ayrı bir uygulamayla test etmesi bu açıdan önemli bir strateji değişikliğine işaret ediyor. Özellikle Direct'in Instagram hesabı olmayan kişiler tarafından da kullanılabilmesi, uygulamanın daha geniş bir kapsamlı bir mesajlaşma hizmetine dönüşmesinin önünü açabilir.
Bu durum Direct'i aynı zamanda Meta'nın diğer mesajlaşma platformu WhatsApp ile kısmen karşı karşıya getirebilir. Direct'in WhatsApp'ın yerini alması pek mümkün olmasa da, Instagram kullanmayan kişilerin de uygulamaya katılabilmesi, Meta'nın mesajlaşma ekosistemi içinde kullanıcıların geçirdiği zamanı farklı uygulamalar arasında yeniden dağıtabilir.
Meta, Direct'i şu aşamada yalnızca Türkiye ve Tayland 'da gerçekleştirilen bir test olarak konumlandırıyor. Şirket uygulamanın başka ülkelere açılıp açılmayacağına ilişkin henüz bir takvim paylaşmış değil. Testin başarılı olması halinde Direct'in daha geniş bir kullanıcı kitlesine sunulması gündeme gelebilir.

FILE - A freight train runs on rails of a railway link of the Crimean Bridge connecting Russian mainland and Crimean peninsula over the Kerch Strait not far from Kerch, Crimea, on Monday, July 17, 2023. AP Photo//AP hide caption
A Ukrainian drone and missile attack prepared over several weeks struck a vital Russian rail and road bridge to the occupied Crimean Peninsula, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Tuesday, in a stunning blow after nearly five years of war.
Zelenskyy portrayed the "unprecedented" operation on the Kerch Bridge as a masterstroke, as Ukrainian forces gradually wore down Russian air defenses before bombarding the prized target with missiles and drones overnight.
He didn't detail the damage but unconfirmed media reports said that a span of the bridge collapsed in the attack, in what would be an embarrassing setback for Moscow.
The Russian-installed governor of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, said that traffic across the bridge has been halted and urged people "to refrain from trips in the direction of the bridge." He didn't mention any damage.
The Kerch Bridge is a crucial link in moving military and civilian supplies from Russia to Crimea and to support troops on the front line. The construction of the bridge, a potent symbol of Russia's illegal annexation of the peninsula in 2014, was inflammatory for Ukrainians.
Moscow's forces, meanwhile, fired ballistic missiles and drones at Kyiv, hitting two of the Ukrainian capital's main bridges and killing at least two people.
A recent escalation in aerial attacks came as Russia and Ukraine await a date for the next round of U.S.-mediated talks aimed at ending the war that began with Moscow's full-scale invasion of its neighbor on Feb. 24, 2022.
U.S. President Donald Trump says he plans to talk about the war in Ukraine during his highly anticipated meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in China this week.
The Kerch Bridge attack was the culmination of weeks of preparatory strikes over seven stages of the operation, Zelenskyy said on social media.
Ukrainian forces knocked out defense systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment and other designated targets before launching Monday night's final attack, he said.
Domestically developed long-range drones struck the bridge's road section during the night while Ukraine's Neptune missiles and other drones aimed at the rail section, he said. Flamingo precision-guided missiles delivered the final blow, he said.
Russia's Investigative Committee said that the bridge was attacked by drones on both days and sustained damage. It didn't elaborate on the extent of the damage.
Zelenskyy noted that Russia has battered Ukrainian infrastructure, especially the power grid, every day.
"We have repeatedly offered Russia steps toward de-escalation — and every proposal has been met with loud rejection," he said.
Russian air defenses downed 1,441 drones during a second straight night of major Ukrainian attacks, Russia's Defense Ministry said Tuesday.
On Monday, Russia said that it downed 1,336 Ukrainian drones in the highest number of interceptions it had reported so far during the war.
Elsewhere, authorities in Bashkortostan, a Russian region in the south of Russia's Ural Mountains, said that defenses repelled a "massive" drone attack on industrial zones of the cities of Ufa and Salavat. All plants there worked as usual, and no critical damage has been inflicted on them, officials said.
Independent news outlet Astra, however, reported a huge fire at the Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat oil refining and petrochemical complex, located nearly 1,300 kilometers (800 miles) east of the Ukrainian border. The complex has been attacked a number of times before.
In Moscow, Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that around 800 drones flew toward the Moscow region overnight. Most were downed far away, and 321 were shot down as they approached the Russian capital.
Experts are inspecting Kyiv's North and South bridges, damaged in a Russian ballistic missile attack, to assess the extent of the destruction, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Tuesday morning.
Russian attacks damaged other infrastructure and started fires in four districts of the Ukrainian capital, officials said, as Moscow continues its campaign to make life difficult for Ukrainian civilians.
The Russian Defense Ministry said Tuesday that its forces overnight carried out a major strike using land- and air-based precision weapons and drones on Ukraine's military industrial facilities, energy, transport and port infrastructure, as well as vessels used for Ukraine's armed forces.
Russian forces launched a combined attack on industrial facilities in three districts of the southern Ukraine region of Zaporizhzhia, killing two people and wounding 18 others and leaving a large number of consumers in the region without power, said Mykhailo Semikin, head of the Zaporizhzhia Regional Military Administration.
Meanwhile, the negotiating teams of Ukraine, the United States, and European partners held a working video call on Monday, during which they discussed the results of recent talks in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, and the agenda for the next stage of negotiations, said Rustem Umerov, head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service.
"We aligned our positions and our next joint steps," Umerov said on Telegram following the conversation.
On the European side, representatives of France, Germany, the United Kingdom, Italy, Poland, NATO and the European Commission joined the conversation.
The United States was represented by envoys Steve Witkoff, Jared Kushner, and Alexus Grynkewich, the commander of U.S. forces in Europe, Umerov said.

The IRGC says the attack is part of efforts to counter ‘hostile activities of US forces in the region’.
Bahraini air defence has thwarted a drone attack, according to the Gulf country’s state television, after Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) launched a barrage of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs).
The IRGC said on Tuesday the “precision operation” targeted a US radar system at the Isa airbase in Bahrain. The attack was “part of efforts to counter the hostile activities of US forces in the region”, it added, according to a statement carried by Iran’s state broadcaster IRIB.
In a statement later on Tuesday, the US military said the attack drones “were intercepted without any damage to U.S. equipment or injury to American personnel”.
Blasts echoed over the Bahraini capital, Manama, after residents received a mobile phone alert warning of a “potential threat”. Explosions were heard after the Ministry of Interior’s alert urged residents to “proceed to the nearest safe location”. It later issued an “all clear” message.
In a statement, the ministry said “precautionary measures remain in place” and urged the public to exercise caution.
The attacks in Bahrain – home to the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet – come amid stalled diplomatic efforts to end the US-Israel war ⁠on Iran, which began ⁠on February 28 and has affected the entire Gulf region and beyond.
Also on Tuesday, Iran’s Foreign Ministry denied a CNN report quoting unnamed sources that it potentially planned to detonate “a dirty bomb” in Washington, DC. The ministry’s spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said on X that the allegations were “baseless”.
In recent days, Iran has claimed attacks on US radar systems Bahrain.
On Sunday, the IRGC launched six drones at a US air defence radar system at Bahrain’s Riffa airbase, which hosts US forces, in response to what it described as hostile US actions.
On Friday, the IRGC also claimed to have targeted a US early-warning radar system in Bahrain, but the US military denied that the facility had been hit, saying it intercepted two Iranian drones without damage or casualties.
“Since Friday, it seems that the rules of engagement have changed,” said Al Jazeera’s Resul Serdar, reporting from Tehran, stating that a pattern has emerged, with Iran now trying to restore deterrence.
“First, Iran warned that if the US escorts ships carrying oil that do not coordinate with Iran [through the Strait of Hormuz], then Tehran would attack US military installations. Now, Iran is saying its attack on a US radar system in Bahrain is because of the US’s continued violations of Iranian airspace.
It is not a response to a specific US attack, but rather the continued violation of its airspace.”
Bahrain has faced renewed security concerns amid escalating tensions between Washington and Tehran.

Ticaret Bakanlığından yapılan yazılı açıklamada, Kurulun tüketicileri aldatan, bilgi ve tecrübe eksikliklerini istismar eden ve haksız rekabete yol açan reklamlar ile ticari uygulamalara yönelik incelemeleri titizlikle yürüttüğü belirtildi.
Kurulun son toplantısını 12 Kasım'da yaptığı ifade edilerek, burada görüşülen dosyalardan 22'sinde inceleme konusu tanıtımların mevzuata aykırı olmadığının değerlendirildiği, 141 dosyanın karara bağlandığı, incelemeler sonucunda mevzuata aykırılık tespit edilen 119 dosyada durdurma cezası uygulandığı bildirildi.
Toplantıda, tüketicileri yanıltıcı reklamlar ile haksız ticari uygulamalara ilişkin 35,9 milyon lira para cezası uygulanmasının kararlaştırıldığı belirtildi.
Toplantıda indirimli satış reklamlarının öne çıktığı bilgisi verilen açıklamada, şunlar ifade edildi:
"Yapılan incelemelerde, bir firmanın mağazasında satışa sunulan bütün ürünlerde tüm tüketicilere her gün yüksek oranlarda indirim uygulandığı yönünde reklamlar yayımladığı, ancak bu indirim vaatlerini gerçeğe uygun şekilde yerine getirdiğini ispatlayamadığı tespit edilmiştir. Tüketicilerde sürekli ve yüksek oranlı indirim yapıldığı algısı oluşturarak, satın alma kararlarını etkileyen söz konusu reklamların yanıltıcı nitelikte olduğu değerlendirilmiştir. Bu kapsamda ilgili firma hakkında 5 milyon lira ceza uygulanmasına ve reklamların durdurulmasına karar verilmiştir."
Mobil iletişim sektöründeki tarife ve taahhüt sürelerine ilişkin tanıtımların da Bakanlıkça yakından takip edildiği belirtilen açıklamada, Reklam Kurulunca yapılan incelemelerde, mobil telefon tarifelerinin "12 ay" veya "12 fatura dönemi" gibi ifadelerle tanıtılmasına rağmen fiili taahhüt sürelerinin tüketicilerin makul beklentilerini karşılamadığının belirlendiği bildirildi.
Açıklamada, "Yapılan değerlendirmelerde, tüketicilerin abonelik başlangıcından itibaren 1 yıl boyunca aynı tarifeden yararlanacakları beklentisiyle işlem gerçekleştirdikleri, ancak fatura kesim tarihine bağlı olarak yalnızca 1 günlük kullanımın dahi ayrı bir fatura dönemi kabul edilebildiği ve bu nedenle taahhüt süresinin fiilen bir aya yakın kısalabildiği tespit edilmiştir." ifadesi kullanıldı.
Tüketicilere sunulan süre algısı ile hizmetin fiili taahhüt süresi arasındaki farklılığın, aldatıcı ve yanıltıcı nitelikte olduğunun değerlendirildiği, söz konusu tanıtımlara ilişkin durdurma cezası uygulanmasına karar verildiği bildirildi.
Taksitlendirme imkanlarına ilişkin tanıtımların da Kurulun inceleme başlıkları arasında yer aldığı belirtilen açıklamada, ilgili mevzuat uyarınca taksitlendirme kısıtlamasına tabi ürünlerle taksitlendirme yapılabilen ürünlerin aynı alışveriş kapsamında birlikte satın alınması halinde alışverişin tamamına taksit uygulanamayacağına işaret edildi.
Kurul tarafından yapılan incelemede, bir firmanın mağaza içinde taksit imkanına ilişkin tanıtımlarında, söz konusu ürünlerin aynı alışveriş kapsamında birlikte satın alınması durumunda taksitlendirme yapılamayacağına ilişkin bilgilendirmeye yer verilmediğinin tespit edildiği, tüketicilerin satın alma kararlarını etkileyebilecek nitelikteki eksik bilgilendirmeler nedeniyle ilgili reklamlara ilişkin durdurma cezası uygulanmasına karar verildiği belirtildi.
Elektronik ticarette ürünlere yönelik yorumlar ve puanlamaların da tüketicilerin satın alma kararlarında önemli rol oynadığına dikkatin çekildiği açıklamada, şunlar kaydedildi:
"Tüketici değerlendirmelerinin güvenilir, şeffaf ve doğru bilgilendirmeye dayalı şekilde sunulması Bakanlığımızın öncelikli denetim alanları arasında bulunmaktadır. Reklam Kurulu tarafından gerçekleştirilen incelemelerde, bir elektronik ticaret pazar yerinde satışa sunulan çeşitli ürünlere yönelik yurt dışından yüksek sayıda yıldız ve puanlama şeklinde değerlendirme yapıldığı, ancak söz konusu değerlendirmelerin yurt dışından gerçekleştirildiğine ilişkin tüketicilere herhangi bir bilgilendirme sunulmadığı tespit edilmiştir. Tüketici memnuniyeti, tüketim eğilimleri ve alışkanlıklarının ülkeler arasında farklılık gösterebileceği dikkate alınarak, değerlendirmelerin kaynağına ilişkin bu eksikliğin tüketicilerin satın alma tercihlerini yanıltabilecek nitelikte olduğu sonucuna varılmıştır. Söz konusu uygulama, haksız ticari uygulama olarak değerlendirilerek, ilgili dosya hakkında idari ceza uygulanmasına karar verilmiştir."

Hundreds of people have been arrested in heated demonstrations against Donald Trump in Manila, as the US president arrived in the city for a leaders’ summit.
Organisers claimed as many as 10,000 people would be joining protests against Trump in the capital of the Philippines on Tuesday, where he is attending the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit. The crowds were expected to try to march to the summit site.
Authorities have arrested nearly 300 people in widespread protests in held in the days leading up to the summit, with large parts of the capital closed off and tight security in place.
Some burned effigies of Trump and faced off with police officers armed with batons and shields. Slogans on placards called the American leader the world’s “No 1 terrorist” in protests held on Monday.
Demonstrators angry at the cost of living and energy shock caused by the Iran war, and the new US-led Pax Silica initiative on AI and critical minerals, tried to reach the summit at the Philippine International Convention Center on Monday, but were blocked by police.
Pax Silica has sparked tensions in the Philippines over plans to build a tech hub outside Manila that critics say will affect water and energy supplies, and displace members of the Ayta Indigenous community.
Large sections of central Manila were closed to the public as part of the security cordon and public holidays put in place for the Asean summit.
After departing from Fairbanks in Alaska, Trump emerged from Air Force One at Ninoy Aquino International airport at 5.54pm local time (0954 GMT), live video showed.
Trump will meet with the leaders of Australia, Japan and India on Tuesday night before heading to Shenzhen in China on Wednesday. There he will attend the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit and hold trilateral talks with China’s president, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin of Russia.
The backlash against Trump follows the ousting of the boss of Nvidia, Jensen Huang, and allegations members of the US administration, including the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, knew about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Protest leader Renato Reyes blamed the arrests in Manila on the heavy handed response of the government on the president, Ferdinand Marcos Jr, calling Monday the largest single day of police arrests since Marcos came to office in 2022.
“It is really crazy that the Philippine government is rolling out the red carpet for someone who has been so flatly rejected by the American people,” Reyes said. “Trump started a war that devastated the global economy and pushed oil prices in the Philippines to historic highs. It has caused untold suffering on the Filipino people.
“So, yes, Trump will have to pay for his crimes and he will have to be answerable, not just to the American people, but to the people of the world.”
The Philippine national police said some officers were injured during confrontations with demonstrators opposed to the summit, including when objects were allegedly thrown at officers.
Pax Silica will include a technology hub planned at New Clark City in Tarlac, about 100km from Manila.
Intended to bolster western stocks of AI technology and reduce “excessive dependencies” on single source supply chains, including from China, Pax Silica will provide chips and critical minerals to 26 participating signatory governments.
Amnesty International said demonstrations should not be forcibly or violently dispersed.
“Reports of arrests during the protests demand immediate scrutiny,” Amnesty’s director for the Philippines, Ritz Lee Santos III, said. “Authorities must explain the specific grounds for each arrest and any continued detention. Anyone detained solely for peacefully exercising their rights must be released immediately.”

So You Are competing in the Melbourne Cup at Flemington Racecourse on 3 November
The body of a top Australian racehorse has been found dumped in a skip bin, hours after its trainer revealed the horse had died from colic.
In a video shared online, only two weeks after So You Are raced in the Melbourne Cup, the deceased racehorse appeared to be lying in a large metal bin surrounded by other household rubbish in Sydney.
Trainer Bjorn Baker - who shared news of the horse's death from colic on Monday - has said he was "deeply distressed" by the video, and called for a "full explanation".
Racing NSW, the state's industry regulator, said a preliminary investigation had found the horse was later properly buried, but called the way its body was handled "completely unacceptable".
"Like everyone who has seen the footage, I am deeply distressed by the handling of So You Are's remains," Baker said in an statement shared online.
"He was a much-loved horse, and he deserved to be treated with dignity and respect after his death."
So You Are had a successful run during spring, winning four times at respected races including the Rosehill, Randwick and the Bendigo Cup.
The five-year-old recently finished eight in the Melbourne Cup, which was won by Point of Law, a horse previously owned by King Charles III.
The racehorse had received urgent treatment after a severe bout of colic, but was "unfortunately unable to be saved" and was euthanised under anaesthesia, Racing NSW said.
"So You Are was then transported for burial, and was being held temporarily, awaiting burial, when these images were recorded," it said.
Burial at a licensed landfill is typically recommended for animals that die from euthanasia due to the chemicals involved in the process, according to the racing body.
"That burial, however, should have occurred in a timely and respectful manner," it added.
In a statement, REC Equine Specialists - the hospital where the horse died - said a contractor had been hired to dispose of the So You Are's body.
"We did not carry out the burial ourselves, but we chose the provider and the arrangements, and we take full responsibility for that."
"We have spoken with So You Are's owners and trainer to apologise personally."
The company added that it had stopped using the contractor, and was reviewing its processes to make sure they known exactly how horses are handled after leaving their hospital.
"No owner should have to go through what So You Are's connections have experienced this week. We will make sure it does not happen again."
Jowett's video appeared to be filmed at a public rubbish drop-off and land facility called Lucas Heights, in Sutherland Shire, south of Sydney.
The waste management company that runs the landfill site said So You Are's body had been moved to a skip bin in a permitted area, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation has reported.

Car seats had some pretty humble beginnings. Even I, an early-’90s baby, slightly recoil every time I see a picture of myself strapped into a flimsy plastic bucket with a loud geometric-print cover that once held my life in its clutches. Car seat design and safety standards have come a long way, and today’s models are quite souped up, with cup holders, rotating bases, and enough bells and whistles to rival an Escalade. And now, they’re getting smart.
Many car seat manufacturers are adding technology to, for lack of a better term, give parents a second set of eyes. Think Bluetooth-connected chest clips, sensors, apps, and real-time alerts that ping your phone if something goes awry, whether that’s an installation issue or if a chest clip comes unbuckled while the car’s moving.
It sounds appealing, right? Especially for parents who already have plenty to worry about and are often juggling a million things just to get out the door in the morning. But it’s worth asking: Do these features actually make car seats safer? Or are parents paying for peace of mind?
I tested two smart car seats, the Babyark Classic ($799) and the Cybex Cloud G Pro ($550) , to see if this technology lives up to the hype and whether a smart seat is worth adding to your registry. Because while an app-connected car seat might seem cool and offer some reassurance, no amount of technology can replace proper installation and use. Keep in mind that they’re not exactly apples-to-apples comparisons; the Babyark is a convertible car seat designed to grow with your little one, while the Cybex is an infant carrier. I tested the Babyark with my toddler daughter and the Cybex with my infant son, giving me a chance to see how each one worked at different stages of parenthood. But both offer a glimpse into how companies are integrating technology into car seats, and I wanted to see how they perform in everyday life.
Many smart car seats revolve around sensors. Some come equipped with sensors that help caregivers determine if the seat is installed correctly. Others use Bluetooth-enabled chest clips to send notifications to your phone if the chest clip breaks free mid-ride or if you walk away from your car while your child is still buckled in. A few models even have crash detection, which can send notifications to designated emergency contacts if a collision is detected.
The biggest difference comes down to how the technology is integrated. Some models, like the Cybex I tested, rely on a Bluetooth chest clip that connects to an app. Babyark takes a slightly different approach, with mechanical indicators on its Classic model and a swankier electronic sensor system built into the base of its higher-end Smart and Premium models.
The first thing I noticed about the Babyark out of the box was its base setup, which was different from any other car seats I’ve used. The base is a spaceship-looking device with a fold-out support leg and anti-rebound bar. The seat itself is pretty bulky, but I didn’t mind too much, since by the time I started using it, my daughter was old enough that I didn’t need to haul her around in an infant seat anymore.
Car seat installation can be an exercise in patience, but I found setup pretty straightforward. The Babyark app walked me through every step, with video tutorials for each stage. Once everything was in place, indicators on the base glowed green. (Red means something’s off.)
The app is easy to navigate, but once I installed the seat, I pretty much forgot about it. I enabled notifications in case something needed attention, but in my several months of using the seat, nothing has warranted an alert so far, aside from the occasional random disconnection.
It’s worth noting that the Babyark offers different versions of the seat, all with different technology. The Classic model, which I have, currently retails at $790 and offers guided installation videos and mechanical indicators. Babyark's Smart and Premium models—which retail for $999 and $1,190, respectively—add features like forgotten child alerts and impact detection. That’s a roughly $200 to $400 jump, which is worth considering if you’re particularly interested in those features.
You can check the app for basic statistics, like how much time your child spends in the seat, but I haven’t felt the need to follow this closely. More importantly, I didn’t find myself opening the app to monitor the seat while my daughter was in it. At the end of the day, the Babyark feels like a regular car seat to me. But a great, sturdy car seat at that!
I also tried out the Cloud G Pro, which comes with SensorSafe, a Bluetooth chest clip that communicates with the Cybex app on your phone. Pairing the clip, which looks and functions like any other, with my phone was easy peasy. When I intentionally tested the alerts, they worked as expected and came through almost immediately.
The temperature notifications worked, but almost too well. SensorSafe sends an alert when your car’s interior climbs to above 95 degrees Fahrenheit or drops below 45. Depending on the weather, your car might already be outside that range when you first get in, and it takes a little time for the cabin to warm up or cool down. So don’t be surprised if you get an alert before the AC or heat has a chance to do its thing.
SensorSafe can also alert you if the clip becomes unbuckled while driving or if you leave your child buckled in the seat and walk away with your phone. In the latter scenario, the default setting has your phone loudly announce “CHILD IN CAR!” in a man’s deep voice, which scared the hoots out of me the first time it went off. If you don’t respond to the alert (you can stop or snooze it), the app will notify your emergency contact and share your location.
Like the Babyark, I didn’t find myself opening the Cybex app very often to check on things. I mostly let it run in the background and waited for notifications rather than actively checking in on the system. The alerts worked just fine, but I used the app so infrequently that my phone eventually offloaded it.
As appealing as all those gadgets and gizmos sound, car seats aren’t foolproof. “These are supplements. They're not substitutes,” says Jennifer Booge, a car seat safety expert with the National Safety Council . “We have to make sure that we're understanding how to use the car seat correctly, because there is so much to know, and every car seat is so different.”
According to data collected through the NSC’s National Digital Car Seat Check Form , a little over 72 percent of car seats entered into the system have some form of misuse. Manufacturers are working to address these issues with installation videos and app-based guidance, but Booge says there’s still not enough research to determine whether smart features actually improve safety.
Some car seat manufacturers offer access to certified child passenger safety technicians who can walk you through installation questions. I experienced this firsthand with the Babyark. Even after following the app’s instructions and getting the green light that everything was secure, I still had some reservations about how much the seat was wiggling. I reached out to the company, and they virtually walked me through the installation. (Which turned out to be correct; car seats are supposed to have a slight wiggle, no more than an inch back and forth.)
“Don't be afraid to pick up the phone and call or schedule that virtual appointment and meet with those experts that are there to help you, because it's not easy,” Booge says. “Every car seat is different. Every vehicle and car seat combination is different.”
As Booge points out, tech can be useful even when it isn’t built into the seat itself. The rise of virtual appointments gives caregivers access to certified technicians that they may not otherwise have available. At the end of the day, a car seat doesn’t need a battery or an app to do its job, and all the technology in the world can’t replace knowing how to use it pr…

Blasts echoed over the Bahraini capital Manama on Tuesday, as Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they launched a drone attack, the third in five days after a weeks-long lull.
Bahrain's armed forces intercepted "Iranian aerial attacks in the kingdom's skies", according to state television, while Iran's Guards said they targeted a US-operated radar system.
Bahrain's Interior Ministry, in a post on X, warned of a "possible threat" and called on the country's residents to remain calm, move to the nearest safe place and follow only official sources for information on developments.
Bahraini officials also said the country's air defence systems had intercepted attacks from Iran.
No confirmed report has yet been released on any impact of Iranian drones on the radar system at Sheikh Isa base or on the extent of any possible damage.
The public relations arm of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps described the pre-dawn attack on Tuesday as a response to what it called "the continued violation of the airspace of the Islamic Republic of Iran" by US military drones.
It said the operation formed part of ongoing air-defence and electronic warfare measures to track, destroy and capture US drones of the MQ and MQM-170 series.
"Combat drones belonging to the Revolutionary Guards carried out a precision operation this morning, targeting a radar system operated by US forces at the Sheikh Isa Air Base in Bahrain," the Guards' Sepah news website said.
The Guards also warned that continued use of regional bases and military facilities for actions against Iran would not go unanswered.
Bahrain was heavily targeted earlier in the war, which started in February, but had been peaceful for weeks until an Iranian drone attack on Friday. A second followed on Sunday.
Friday's strike was the first Iranian attack against a Gulf country since early September.
The US military said it had shot down two drones launched Friday by Iranian forces, while the Bahraini army said it had intercepted Sunday's attack.
Bahrain, which hosts a major US naval base, has experienced numerous Iranian attacks since US-Israeli strikes on Iran triggered the Middle East war in February.
Since September, the conflict has mainly been restricted to the area around the strategic Strait of Hormuz, with the US blockading Iranian ports and Tehran attempting to control the oil shipping route.
The Middle East war will be on the agenda during an unprecedented trilateral summit between US President Donald Trump and his Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, scheduled this week in China, according to the White House.
As talks aimed at ending the war appear to be deadlocked, a third US aircraft carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, is operating in the Middle East, the US military said on Monday.

A Costa Rican journalist who denounced alleged links between politicians and drug traffickers in the Central American country has been shot dead.
Police said gunmen on a motorbike ambushed Camilo Rodríguez, 50, as he was travelling in his car north of the capital, San José, on Monday afternoon.
The independent reporter earlier said he had been receiving death threats from drug trafficking gangs.
Local media reported that it was the first murder of a journalist in more than two decades in Costa Rica. It comes at a time when transnational crime gangs are increasing their presence in the country, driving up its formerly low homicide rate.
The president of the Costa Rican Journalists' Association, Yanancy Noguera, said that "all evidence so far points to the silencing of a dissenting voice in Costa Rica - a person who published information about organised crime in the country".
Rodríguez had been working as a journalist for several decades, both in radio and in print.
Most recently, he had been uploading videos to social media in which he named public figures such as judges, business people and politicians, which he alleged were corrupt or had ties to known drug traffickers.
In one of his videos, he alleged that the home of Costa Rica's President, Laura Fernández, had been constructed by a company that he said had links to a criminal gang.
Fernández, who categorically denied any wrongdoing, took the journalist to court, accusing him of defamation.
Reacting to his murder in a video message, the president strongly condemned the attack, calling it "a stain on freedom of expression".
She added that she had instructed police to do their utmost to "punish Camilo's murderers".
Rodríguez had also tried to stand for political office, seeking to run as the presidential candidate for the Costa Rican Renovation Party in 2021.
However, his candidacy was rejected by the electoral authorities after the party failed to meet the necessary criteria required to file candidates.
Costa Rica's Attorney General, Carlo Díaz, said that "silencing someone who reports on drug trafficking or corruption, in this case a communicator, is a signal we cannot tolerate in a democratic society".
Candidate tough on crime wins Costa Rica presidential election

The United States has confirmed it is investigating computing company Megaspeed, suspecting it of violating US export controls by helping to ship tech giant Nvidia's chips to China.
In a joint statement, the US Department of Justice and Department of Commerce said they had been investigating Singapore-based firm Megaspeed since 2024.
It comes after questions were raised about the possibility high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
Concerns emerged in recent weeks after Nvidia founder Jensen Huang revealed he had an extramarital affair , allegedly with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang. US authorities suspect her of spying for Beijing, which China denies.
Jensen Huang resigned from his role as chief executive last week following revelations he had two affairs.
Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and is suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China. The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.
The justice and commerce departments said on Monday that "it is in the public interest to provide the facts and address inaccurate information" regarding the investigation.
Laying out a timeline, it said it began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations".
In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia "concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed". In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its 'no sell' list.
Agents from the Bureau of Industry and Security, in conjunction with Singaporean law enforcement officials, then conducted an on-site check at Megaspeed that month and interviewed Alice Huang, who was chief executive at the time.
Alice Huang and Jensen Huang pictured together in Taiwan in June 2024
Following this enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed.
The Nvidia scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end chips to Megaspeed.
On Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed the US Commerce Department, led by Howard Lutnick, for failing to properly oversee the export of the chips.
Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.
While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.
Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair.
The White House said on Monday it would further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms like Nvidia.
The reported affairs by Jensen Huang created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a major company in the AI industry and central to the US as it competes with China for dominance.
Trump downplays warnings of AI risks, citing rivalry with China
In the statement, the US government said it would "bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred".
They added: "Sensitive technologies like semiconductors are among the most valuable and strategic assets of the US economy, and the Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce will remain vigilant in pursuing justice for those who want to compromise America's technological edge."
Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says
Nvidia dismisses 'Bring Jensen Back' campaign as Trump backs effort to reinstate ex boss
How the Jensen Huang scandal created a headache for business-friendly Singapore

Protesters hurl bricks, torch vehicles and block the main highway between the capital, Dhaka, and the key financial district, Mymensingh.
Bangladeshi police have fired tear gas and stun grenades at thousands of garment workers protesting after a key wage board meeting was postponed.
Protesters on Tuesday hurled bricks, torched vehicles and blocked the main highway between the capital, Dhaka, and the key financial district of Mymensingh.
Bangladesh is the world’s second-biggest garment exporter behind China, producing clothes for big international brands, including Fruit of the Loom and Levi Strauss.
But growing worker unrest over wages, which began last month, has disrupted the industry that generates $38bn annually and employs more than four million people.
Workers are demanding a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka ($240) – a 140-percent increase on the current 12,500 taka, as they struggle to cope with rising food, housing, transport and healthcare costs.
About 500 of the country’s 4,500 garment factories are shut, sources told the AFP news agency, further stoking unrest among workers.
A “no work, no pay” provision in the country’s labour laws allows factory owners to suspend operations and withhold wages when production is disrupted.
“The owners seem unwilling to meet our salary demands. They are already dragging their feet,” one worker, Khanom, 24, told AFP.
Tensions were also running high in the garment hubs of Savar and Ashulia on Dhaka’s outskirts.
The wage board , comprising representatives of employers and workers, was set up by the government earlier this month to negotiate a pay rise.
The new minimum wage would be announced in December and take effect in January next year.
“We want to return to our machines,” garment worker Rakib, 28, told AFP.
“We are not sure if the wage board members are aware of our demands,” he said, adding that workers feared their concerns might not be reflected in the revised wage proposal.
Most factories had opened on Tuesday morning, but were shut down as protests spread to the highway, Rakib said.
In a joint statement, the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) and the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BKMEA) called for a resumption of wage negotiations as soon as possible.
A wage board meeting scheduled for Monday was postponed after a member representing the garment workers said he was unwell, a BGMEA source told AFP.
The next meeting would be held on November 23, the board said.
In the wake of Tuesday’s protest, Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) stepped up patrols across the industrial zone, deploying hundreds of personnel.
“BGB headquarters has been closely observing the situation from a monitoring cell,” it said in a statement.
The force said it was also using drones, body-worn cameras and other devices to keep a close watch on demonstrations.

The body of a horse that placed eighth in Australia’s Melbourne Cup two weeks ago and recently fell ill has been found dumped in skip bin in Sydney.
The horse So You Are, a five-year-old gelding, was put down after it suffered from a severe bout from colic and was taken to hospital on Monday for surgery.
The same day, Gregg Jowett posted to his personal social media account a video that showed a dead horse inside a skip bin in Sydney. Guardian Australia has chosen not to publish the video.
“I’m at the tip. It’s a fucking horse. They tipped a horse in the fucking bin at the tip,” he can be heard saying in the video.
“[I’m] quite shocked about that; that’s not normal. Please let me know if I’m wrong, but that’s not normal.”
Jowett later told Guardian Australia he didn’t know when he found the horse that it was So You Are, or a horse that had competed in Australia’s most famous race, the Melbourne Cup.
The horse’s trainer, Bjorn Baker, said the handling of So You Are’s remains had compounded an already devastating loss.
“Like everyone who has seen the footage, I am deeply distressed by the apparent handling of So You Are’s remains,” he said in a statement.
“He was a much-loved horse, and he deserved to be treated with dignity and respect after his death.
“I understand the hospital facility REC Equine Specialists are investigating the circumstances, and I expect a full explanation of what occurred.
“My thoughts remain with [So You Are breeders] the Ramsey family, and with all my staff, for whom this has compounded an already devastating loss.”
Dr Jonathan Lumsden, the managing partner of REC Equine Specialists, which treated So You Are after he was brought to the service with colic, apologised “unreservedly for the distress caused by footage shared on social media today”.
“Despite the best efforts of our veterinary team, he could not be saved and was humanely euthanised under anaesthesia,” Lumsden said.
“After his death, So You Are was collected by our contracted provider and taken to a licensed landfill. He should have been promptly and respectfully buried.
“What happened was unacceptable and disrespectful to So You Are and to everyone who cared for him. We are deeply sorry.
“So You Are was in our care. We did not carry out the burial ourselves, but we chose the provider and the arrangements, and we take full responsibility for that. We should have known exactly how horses were handled after leaving our hospital, and we did not. That process is not good enough, and it must change.
“We have spoken with So You Are’s owners and trainer to apologise personally,” he said. “We are working with our disposal provider and the facility operators, together with Racing NSW, to establish how this happened and to put in processes to ensure it never happens again.”
Lumsden said the service had, effective immediately, stopped using the contract provider and was undertaking a review of how other providers care for horses after death.
“Out of respect for So You Are and those who loved him, we ask that the footage not be shared further,” Lumsden said.
David Harris, the minister for gaming and racing, said Racing NSW had launched an investigation into the incident.
“This is a concerning incident, the racing legislative framework and Racing NSW as the sport’s controlling body has measures in place to safeguard racing integrity and animal welfare,” he said.
Georgie Purcell, the Animal Justice party MP for northern Victoria, said the incident should “force serious questions the industry’s so-called duty of care”.
“The racing industry breeds these horses and profits for them but fails the most basic obligation to treat them with dignity after death,” she said.
