Watch: As new Bond, Pattinson takes on one of film's most high-profile roles
Robert Pattinson, the British actor known for films such as Twilight and The Batman, has been confirmed as the next actor to play James Bond.
The announcement was made by Amazon MGM Studios in a social media post on Monday, with a picture showing Pattinson in character as 007.
The 40-year-old becomes the seventh actor to play the famous fictional spy and will star in the 26th Bond movie, due to be released in 2028.
In a statement, the London-born actor said: "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime."
The next Bond film will be directed by Denis Villeneuve and written by Steven Knight, but its title and exact release date have not yet been announced.
In his statement, Pattinson said he was "deeply grateful" to the film's creative team "for their belief in me".
"To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement," he added. "I couldn't be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team."
The announcement comes after years of intense speculation about who will take over from Daniel Craig in one of the most high-profile - and highly scrutinised - roles in entertainment.
The next 007 film will be the first since long-term Bond producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson stepped back and Amazon took creative control of the franchise, after acquiring the series' parent company MGM.
By the time the 26th Bond film is released, it will have been seven years since the last - 2021's No Time To Die - the biggest gap in the franchise's history.
'Big shoes to fill': Robert Pattinson asked about playing Bond in 2010
Director Villeneuve is best known for films including the Dune trilogy, Prisoners, Sicario, Arrival and Blade Runner 2049, while writer Knight is known for TV hits Peaky Blinders and House of Guinness, and films including Burnt, Spencer and Locke.
Pattinson has already worked with Villeneuve on Dune: Part 3, where he stars as a new villain, Scytale. The film is released next month.
In a statement reacting to Pattinson's Bond casting, Villeneuve said: "Before anything else, I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey.
"We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007. I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond.
"He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin."
Robert Pattinson has starred in Twilight, Tenet, The Batman and The Odyssey
Pattinson's casting was also welcomed by Buckingham Palace, with a post on Instagram sharing the news and adding: "Welcome to His Majesty's Secret Service, Mr Bond."
Australian actor George Lazenby, who played James Bond in the 1969 film On Her Majesty's Secret, posted a video on social media welcoming Pattinson to "the most exclusive club in the world".
"Remember to enjoy yourself... Let's see if you'll have 'this never happened to the other fella' moment," Lazenby said.
Several other actors, including Josh O'Connor, Callum Turner and Jack Lowden, were reported to be in the frame for the role as screen tests took place in recent weeks.
But Amazon MGM ultimately went with a household name, choosing a more bankable movie star who is widely seen as a safe pair of hands.
Producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman said the "legacy of James Bond is in great hands with Robert Pattinson".
"His fearlessness as an actor, his self-deprecating wit and his ability to continually reinvent himself make him the perfect Bond for our times."
At 40, Pattinson is one of the older actors who was thought to have auditioned for the role of Bond.
Reports last week suggested Pattinson's deal committed him to playing 007 for three films, , external rather than the four that had reportedly been discussed with some of the other actors, but that has not been officially confirmed.
Pattinson shot to fame in Harry Potter and went on to star in Twilight opposite Kristen Stewart (pictured in 2011)
Robert Pattinson shot to fame as Cedric Diggory in 2005's Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire.
He went on to play vampire Edward Cullen in Twilight, the hugely popular film series based on Stephenie Meyer's best-selling novels.
Pattinson starred opposite Kristen Stewart in five Twilight films in total, which collectively made more than $3bn (£2.2bn) at the box office worldwide.
He has gone on to star in other major films such as 2022's The Batman and Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey, released earlier this year.
But he is also respected within the industry for how many roles he has taken in smaller movies - often independent, experimental or arthouse films.
His other credits include The Lighthouse, Mickey 17, Life, The Drama, Good Time, The Rover, Bel Ami, Primetime, Tenet and The Lost City of Z.
Pattinson follows in the footsteps of only six actors to have played James Bond in the official film series – Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig.
Daniel Craig was a popular 007 and appeared in five James Bond films
Craig appeared in five Bond movies in total, starting with 2006's Casino Royale, and spent 16 years as the secret agent created by author Ian Fleming.
In a statement, Fleming's estate said they were "delighted to welcome Robert Pattinson to the James Bond family".
The next film will mark a new era for the franchise. Amazon purchased MGM for $8.5bn in 2021, which included the rights to distribute James Bond.
Then in 2025, long-time Bond producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson agreed to sell creative control of the franchise to Amazon MGM.
Before that, the franchise had been under the Broccoli family's control since 1962's Dr. No, when Sean Connery first starred as Bond.
The Broccoli family preserved the integrity of the character and brand for decades, resisting spin-offs and licensing that some industry experts now expect to see following Amazon's takeover.

A Milli Futbol Takımı , UEFA Uluslar Ligi A Ligi'ne veda etti. Yunanistan'ın Volos'ta Sırbistan'ı 1-0 yenmesi, Türkiye'nin B Ligi'ne düştüğünü kesinleştirdi. Fransa , Belçika ve İtalya 'nın bulunduğu grupta 6 maçta puan alamayan milliler, -11 averajla Çekya'nın ardından düşen ikinci takım oldu. Sırbistan ise averaj üstünlüğü sayesinde A Ligi'nde kalmak için play-out oynayacak.
Türkiye'nin kaderi, Volos'taki Panthessaliko Stadı'nda oynanan Yunanistan - Sırbistan maçına bağlıydı. İlk yarı 0-0 bitti. Maçın tek golü 69. dakikada Giorgos Masouras'tan geldi.
Milliler için play-out kapısı ancak Sırbistan'ın deplasmanda 4-0 ya da daha farklı yenilmesiyle aralanacaktı. Yunanistan tek farklı galibiyetle yetindi ve bu ihtimal ortadan kalktı.
Sırbistan da 6 maçını kaybetti. 4 gol atıp 12 gol yiyen ekip, grubu -8 averajla son sırada tamamladı. Türkiye'nin -11'lik averajının üstünde kalması, Sırbistan'a A Ligi'nde kalmak için play-out oynama hakkı verdi.
Fransa , Belçika ve İtalya ile aynı gruba düşen A Milli Takım , 6 maçta tek puan bile alamadı. 4 gol atıp 15 gol yedi, grubu -11 averajla bitirdi.
Seri, Eylül'de Kocaeli 'de Fransa'ya 1-0 yenilerek başladı. Golü 54. dakikada Mbappe attı. Teknik direktör Vincenzo Montella maçın ardından 'Daha fazlasını hak ediyorduk' demişti. İtalya'ya 4-1, Belçika'ya 3-0 yenilen milliler, sezonun son virajında da puan getiremedi.
15 Kasım'da Bordeaux'da oynanan son maçta Fransa 2-1 kazandı. 49. dakikada Emirhan Topçu'nun kendi kalesine attığı gol skoru açtı, 80. dakikada Kroupi farkı ikiye çıkardı. Abdülkerim Bardakçı 90. dakikada kafayla skoru 2-1'e getirdi ama o kadar. Arda Güler 'in golü ise VAR'a takılmıştı.
UEFA Uluslar Ligi statüsünde A Ligi'ndeki dört grup sonuncusunun en kötü iki takımı doğrudan B Ligi'ne düşüyor. Çekya bu listeye ilk giren ülke oldu, Türkiye de ikinci olarak onu izledi.
Sırbistan ise averajda önde bittiği için bu kaderden kurtuldu. Grubu puansız tamamlamasına rağmen A Ligi'nde kalma şansını play-out maçlarında arayacak.
A Milli Takım yoluna B Ligi'nde devam edecek. Yeni sezondaki rakipler UEFA'nın yapacağı kurayla belli olacak.

Ali Poyrazoğlu birçok tiyatro oyununda oynadı, çeviriler yaptı.
Türk tiyatrosunun duayen isimlerinden Ali Poyrazoğlu , Ceyda Düvenci'nin sunumuyla NTV ekranlarında izleyiciyle buluşan “ Bambaşka Sohbetler ” programına konuk oldu. Birçok konu hakkında konuşan Ali Poyrazoğlu, aynı anda birçok işi birlikte yaptığını anlattı.
Hem tiyatro sahnesinde seyirciyle buluşan hem çeşitli eğitimler veren hem yazı yazan hem çeviri yapan Poyrazoğlu, eğlenmediği hiçbir işi yapmadığını söyledi.
80 yaşındaki Ali Poyrazoğlu, "Eğlenerek sahneye çıktığım, kamera karşısına geçtiğim ve ders verdiğim için kendimi hiç çalışmış görmüyorum. Daha işe başlamadım" dedi.
2022 yılında tiyatrosunun deposunda çıkan yangından ve kaybettiği tablolar, dekorlar ve kukla koleksiyonundan söz eden Ali Poyrazoğlu, “Depoyla beraber birçok şey gitti ama ne yapalım? Biz kaos yönetmeye alışık insanlarız. Yeni baştan toparlamaya başladık” ifadelerini kullandı.
İlişkilerde yapılan hatalardan intikam almaya değil, ders çıkarmaya odaklanmak gerektiğini vurgulan oyuncu, asıl bakılması gereken şeyin karşıdakinin ne yaptığı değil, kişinin kendisinin ne yaptığı olduğunu vurguladı.
Sabah rutininden bahseden Ali Poyrazoğlu, "Her sabah kalkıp spor yapıyorum. Bu işi yaparken hem eğleniyorum hem de ciddiye alıyorum. Sonra gazetelerin manşetlerine bakıyorum, içinde bakmam gereken bir şey varsa girip okuyorum. Bu sırada kahvaltı ediyorum" dedi.
Kahvaltı sonrası kitap okuduğunu da söyleyen Poyrazoğlu, "Okumak şölen gibidir. Çünkü bir kitabı okumaya başlayınca senin yaratıcı evrenin başlar. Bir yazarın yazdıklarıyla bambaşka bir yola çıkarsın" diye konuştu.

Grammy 2027 adaylarında birçok kategoride kadın yıldızlar öne çıkarken, Raye, 11 adaylıkla bu yılın en çok aday gösterilen ismi oldu. İngiliz şarkıcıyı 9 adaylıkla Rosalia takip etti.

Swansea City are increasingly resigned to their head coach, Vítor Matos, joining Strasbourg after he indicated a desire to join Chelsea’s sister club. The Ligue 1 club have approached Swansea with a view to Matos succeeding Hugo Oliveira.
Strasbourg, acquired by Chelsea’s parent company BlueCo in 2023, have identified Matos as a replacement for Oliveira, who has won three of 10 league matches since succeeding Gary O’Neil in July. The French club are hovering two points above the relegation zone.
Matos is under contract until 2030 and Swansea would be due significant compensation for the 38-year-old, a former Liverpool academy and development team coach.
Matos has won admirers since taking charge of Swansea last November and, despite one win in their past five games, has the south Wales club in the Championship playoff spots. Swansea finished last season in 11th and backed Matos in the transfer market this summer in the hope of pushing on.
Swansea’s next match is at home to West Brom on Saturday, before a trip to Middlesbrough and a south Wales derby against Cardiff in the Welsh capital.
Matos, who is due to celebrate a year in charge at Swansea this month, joined the club from Marítimo, a Portuguese second-division club. His 12-game spell in charge of Maritimo represented his first senior management job.
Strasbourg and Chelsea share a close relationship and have traded players, with Emmanuel Emegha and Valentín Barco joining the English club in recent months.
In the most notable move between the clubs, however, Liam Rosenior left his role as Strasbourg head coach to take charge of Chelsea in January, but the former Hull manager was sacked in April . O’Neil succeeded Rosenior but joined Ipswich in June .

Süper Lig ve 1. Lig'in 2027-28 sezonundan başlayacak beş sezonluk yayın hakları için açılan ihalede şartnameyi alan kurumların isimleri ortaya çıktı. Türkiye gazetesinde Tahir Kum'un haberine göre 750 bin TL bedelli şartnameyi altı kurum satın aldı; beIN, Saran- Amazon ortaklığı, Turkcell, Türk Telekom ve TRT bunların arasında. Teklifler 30 Kasım Pazartesi günü noter huzurunda teslim edilecek.
İhale, 2027-28 sezonundan itibaren geçerli olacak hakları kapsıyor ve kapalı teklif ile açık artırma usulüyle yapılacak. TFF'nin 5 Kasım'da duyurduğu paketler şöyle: Paket A Süper Lig yayınını, Paket B 1. Lig yayınını ve iki ligin radyo yayını ile geniş özetlerini, Paket C uluslararası yayını, Paket D uluslararası bahis sitelerinden yayın ile dijital özetleri içeriyor. Paket E ise hepsini tek elde topluyor.
Maçlardan elde edilecek veri hakları ihalenin dışında. TFF ayrıca ihalenin 2886 ve 4734 sayılı kanunlara tabi olmadığını belirtiyor, bütün teklifleri reddetme ya da ihaleyi iptal etme hakkını da saklı tutuyor. Şartnameyi sermaye şirketleri, kamu kurum ve kuruluşları, ortak girişimler ve iş ortaklıkları alabiliyor; bedel TFF'nin banka hesabına yatırıldıktan sonra belgeler Riva'daki Mali İşler Direktörlüğü'nden teslim ediliyor.
Türkiye gazetesinde Tahir Kum'un haberine göre altı kurumun beşi şunlar: beIN, Saran Group ile Amazon 'un ortaklığı, Turkcell, Türk Telekom ve TRT . Altıncı kurumun adı haberde yer almıyor. Şartname almak, o kurumun teklif vereceği anlamına gelmiyor; yayın haklarının kimde kalacağına dair de henüz bir sonuç yok.
Haberin dikkat çeken yanı GSM operatörlerinin yükselişi. Kulislere göre en güçlü aday Turkcell. Operatörlerin başlıca kozu, internet servisleri üzerinden kaçak yayın sitelerine erişimi engelleyerek korsanla mücadeleye katkı sunabilmeleri. Turkcell ve Türk Telekom'un zaten içerik de ürettiği, mobil ve sabit internet abone tabanının ise büyük bir avantaj olarak görüldüğü aktarılıyor. Bunlar resmî bir açıklamaya değil, kulis bilgisine dayanıyor.
TFF, ihale tarihini yaklaşık bir buçuk ay öne çekerek 13 Ocak 2027'den 30 Kasım 2026'ya aldığını duyurdu ve bunun Yayın İhale Komisyonu'nun değerlendirmesi sonucunda yapıldığını belirtti. Teklifler 30 Kasım Pazartesi günü 14.00-14.10 arasında Riva'daki TFF tesislerinde, noter huzurunda ve komisyon önünde teslim edilecek. Türkiye gazetesinin aktardığına göre değişiklikte, ihale ocakta yapılırsa dekoderlerinin üretiminin ve bürokratik işlemlerin yeni sezona yetişemeyecek kadar uzun süreceğini TFF'ye bildiren bir talip etkili oldu; şirketin adı verilmedi.
Hedeflenen gelir 500 milyon dolar olarak aktarılıyor. 2024'teki ihalede masada yalnızca beIN Sports ile Saran Grubu vardı, bu kez listeye iki büyük operatör de girdi. Kapalı tekliflerin ardından açık artırmaya geçilecek; Süper Lig'in 2027'den sonra hangi ekranlarda izleneceği bu iki adımda belli olacak.

Vitor Matos spent five years on Jurgen Klopp's staff at Liverpool
Vitor Matos is close to leaving Swansea City to take charge of French top-flight club Strasbourg.
Strasbourg have made an official approach for the Swansea head coach, who looks likely to depart even though there is no agreement yet between the clubs over a compensation package.
Matos was at Swansea's training ground on Tuesday morning, but is understood to have told the Championship side he wants to leave.
Matos is under contract until 2030, meaning Swansea will be due significant compensation should he depart.
But that has not stopped Strasbourg targeting the 38-year-old Portuguese, who had been due to celebrate a year in charge at Swansea later this month.
Current Strasbourg boss Hugo Oliveira, Matos' fellow countryman, is under pressure after a run of five defeats in six matches.
Oliveira has managed only three wins in 10 league games since succeeding Gary O'Neil - who left to take over at Ipswich Town – in July.
O'Neil led Strasbourg to an eighth-place finish last season, but they are currently 13th in Ligue 1, only two points above the relegation zone.
Strasbourg are a sister club of Premier League side Chelsea.
Matos has turned Swansea from potential relegation contenders to promotion hopefuls since taking charge, with the club 20th in the Championship when he took over last November.
The Swans finished 11th last season and have made further strides in the first third of this campaign.
Vitor Matos led Swansea to seven wins in their first 10 league games of the season, though they have since lost four in five
Matos' team have been among the early-season pacesetters in the second tier, enjoying two spells on top of the table, but their form has dipped in recent weeks.
Swansea have suffered four defeats in their past five matches, though they remain only three points off top spot going into Saturday's home game against West Bromwich Albion.
Matos was touted as a contender to take charge at Crystal Palace earlier this season - the Eagles have since appointed Thomas Frank - while he has also been linked with a return to Portugal on the back of his impact at Swansea.
Listen to the latest Swansea City interviews, news and discussion on BBC Sounds
When asked in October about the Palace links, Matos said: "I'm Swansea manager. I love being here, love my players, love the staff, so my focus is always on the next game and what we can do better."
In an interview last week, Swansea chief executive Tom Gorringe acknowledged that Matos' impact will not have gone unnoticed at other clubs, though he played down the idea of the former Liverpool coach having his head turned.
"The reality is there'll always be interest in anyone performing well in any role on and off the pitch," Gorringe said.
"That's one of the outcomes of being successful - we're aware of that.
"[But] we're all quite happy. We've all agreed to go on this journey together and we hope that Vitor is here a long time."
After West Brom visit, Swansea go to second-placed Middlesbrough next Tuesday before Cardiff City make the short trip west for the first south Wales derby in two seasons on Sunday, 29 November.
Should Matos depart, it is thought likely that a number of his backroom team will also move on.

Tony Mowbray has stepped back from his role as the Blackburn Rovers head coach for health reasons.
The 62-year-old rejoined Rovers in June and has guided a club threatened with relegation last season to 13th in the Championship , three points off the playoff places. However, he has been forced to step away from the game for a second time owing to a health issue.
Mowbray temporarily left his job as Birmingham City’s manager in February 2024 for medical treatment. He resigned three months later for health reasons and later confirmed he had been diagnosed with bowel cancer. Blackburn have not disclosed specifics in relation to Tuesday’s announcement.

Tony Mowbray's final game in charge of Blackburn Rovers was an impressive 2-1 win over West Ham United before November's international break
Blackburn Rovers head coach Tony Mowbray has stepped down from his role with the Championship club amid health issues.
The 62-year-old returned for a second spell in June having previously spent five years managing Rovers between 2017 and 2022.
Mowbray had previously taken time out of the game during his time as Birmingham City boss in early 2024 following a health scare, and later revealed he had been undergoing treatment for bowel cancer.
Rovers said Damien Johnson and Mike Dodds would take responsibility for first-team duties "for the time being".
"Unfortunately, due to health issues, I have to step back from my role as head coach of Blackburn Rovers," Mowbray said in a statement. , external
"I'm immensely proud of this group of players. Their dedication and professionalism have given us some memorable performances and wins, and I've loved working with them.
"Thank you to my coaching staff for all your hard work and for the support you've given me. It's been a pleasure working alongside you.
"To the fans, thank you for the way you've supported me and the team this season. I've always tried to give you a team that you can be proud of. Your support has meant a great deal to me."
Mowbray has transformed Blackburn this season, after a they hovered around the relegation places for much of last term before eventually finishing 20th in the Championship and five points above the drop zone.
They are currently 13th in the Championship table having won six of their 15 league games and three points outside the play-offs.
The announcement comes before Sunday's Lancashire derby against Burnley at Turf Moor, which was set to be Mowbray's 900th game in management as well as his 63rd birthday.
Mowbray has been in management for over two decades and his first spell at Blackburn ended at the conclusion of the 2021-22 season when he was eventually replaced by Jon Dahl Tomasson.
He subsequently held roles with Sunderland, Birmingham and a second spell with West Bromwich Albion before his return to Ewood Park.
In his first spell at Blackburn, he could not halt the club's relegation from the Championship, yet he led them to promotion back from League One at the first attempt and subsequently re-established them in the second tier.
In February 2024, he had been diagnosed with cancer but was eventually given the all-clear following treatment.
He leaves with Blackburn in better shape than they were during a tumultuous 2025-26 campaign, which finished with Michael O'Neill opting not to take the manager's job on a full-time basis and instead choosing to remain as boss of Northern Ireland.
"Tony's passion for the club and his professionalism are clear to see, but it is his kindness and the care he shows for players, staff and those around him that mean so much," Blackburn chief executive officer Steve Curwood added.
"Our priority now is to make sure he feels that same care and support from all of us. We will support him and his family in every way we can."

Declan Rice has agreed a new five-year contract at Arsenal , with the England midfielder poised to match Bukayo Saka’s status as the highest-paid player at the Premier League champions.
Representatives for Rice, who won his 82nd cap in England’s thrilling win over Spain on Sunday, have been in talks for months about extending the deal he signed in 2023 after a record £105m move from West Ham. That is believed to be worth about £250,000 a week and is due to expire in 2028, although Arsenal have the option of a further 12 months.
Rice’s new contract will expire in 2031 and includes a substantial pay rise, rewarding Rice for his status as one of Mikel Arterta’s key players and taking his salary to about £300,000 a week. Saka signed his new five-year contract last season.
Rice was a driving force in Arsenal ending their 22-year wait to be champions in May, although the second half of his campaign was hampered by back and hamstring injuries . The 27-year-old admitted last week he had an “average” World Cup as a result, although he looked back to his best against Spain.
Arsenal have also agreed a contract extension for Jurriën Timber, whose deal is due to expire in 2028. The Dutchman, recently back from a groin injury that forced him to miss the World Cup, has been one of Arteta’s most consistent performers since joining from Ajax in 2023.
The Arsenal manager committed his future by signing a new four-year deal last month that could take him beyond a decade in charge. Arteta and the sporting director, Andrea Berta, have prioritised securing their top players on long-term contracts over the past year and talks are believed to be ongoing with David Raya and Piero Hincapié.
The captain, Martin Ødegaard, is about to enter the final 18 months of his deal but said last weekend that negotiations over an extension had not begun. “I’m happy and hope I can stay there for a long time to come, but we haven’t started on that yet,” he said.

Tony Mowbray has stepped down from his role as Blackburn Rovers head coach due to health issues.
The 62-year-old returned to football at West Brom last year following his recovery from bowel cancer, before taking charge at Blackburn in June.
In a statement, Mowbray said: "Unfortunately, due to health issues, I have to step back from my role as head coach of Blackburn Rovers.

"Thank you to my coaching staff for all your hard work and for the support you've given me. It's been a pleasure working alongside you.

"I'm grateful to the owners and Suhail [Shaikh, Blackburn's chief operating officer] for giving me the opportunity to lead this great club once again.
"I'd ask that you give me and my family privacy at this time.
Mowbray had enjoyed an impressive start to his second spell at Blackburn. Tipped for relegation by many, Rovers currently sit just three points off the play-offs in 13th. In their last game before the international break they beat West Ham 2-1.

Angry captain Andy Robertson says Scotland do not have time to turn things around after a brutal 4-0 defeat by Switzerland consigned them to a third-place finish in their Nations League group.
Head coach Sebastien Pocognoli - appointed as Steve Clarke's successor in August - has consistently stressed the need for patience as he tries to implement a more attack-minded style.
However, the Belgian has won just two of his first six matches in charge, both against North Macedonia, and conceded 10 goals in that time.
They collapsed worryingly easily in St Gallen against a much-changed Swiss outfit on Monday after a promising start, Bologna midfielder Lewis Ferguson putting through his own goal and early intensity gave way to indecision.
The Swiss struck twice in the early minutes of the second half to make it 3-0 and Zeki Amdouni made it four late on.
"First half, I thought we were in the game, we lost a stupid goal, but I thought we had chances and could have been 2-1 at half time," a frustrated Robertson said, on the night he surpassed Kenny Dalglish as his country's most capped men's player.
"By the time you get to 50 minutes and you're 3-0 down, that can't happen in international football.
"It is a really tough night for us. I don't think you've got time in international football, you have to do it.
"These supporters who travel everywhere, are they going to give us time? No. Are the people inside Hampden going to give us time? No. Are the people outside Hampden who are going to be critical and rightly so? No.
"We don't have time, the players do not have time, we have got to step up.
"We have a long break now to March, which is not a good thing, and it is going to be a tough one to swallow."
Robertson eclipses Dalglish to become Scotland's most capped man
This was meant to be a special occasion for Robertson, but it was usurped by the debate over Pocognoli's future.
Just six games into his tenure, there are serious questions being asked over whether the former Union Saint-Gilloise and Monaco coach is capable of delivering on his promise of making Scotland easier on the eye, while delivering positive results.
Tottenham Hotspur left-back Robertson was not the only player to deliver a scathing assessment.
When asked if Scotland were on the right path, John McGinn replied: "Well, obviously the trajectory of the results means it's impossible for me to say yes."
Fellow midfielder Billy Gilmour added: "As a team we know we need to show passion and fight. We've not quite done that tonight."
Supporters are already frustrated at Pocognoli's 3-5-2 formation as they see wingers sidelined or - in the case of Ben Gannon-Doak - shoehorned into an unfamiliar wing-back role.
One man familiar with the difficulties of being the Scotland manager is former boss Craig Levein, who believes the Belgian needs to take a leaf out of his predecessor's book.
"Pocognoli is picking up where Clarke left off," Levein said on BBC Scotland. "In that situation, you need to get off to a good start. That's what the players are looking for - that you're going to make them better.
"I'd be thinking 'we need to stop losing goals'. We haven't got a potent threat, so how do we get results? As Steve recognised, you need to be hard to beat."
In contrast to his deflated players, Pocognoli put on a brave face post-match and insists he sees positive signs after his first two camps.
"The score is heavy with the 4-0, but I don't think it's a reflection of the game," he said.
"We played a good first half, we created chances, we were dominant in some moments, and we faced Switzerland with different shapes and adapted well from the first minute. We conceded from maybe one of the first chances they had.
"At the end, it's a bad feeling, the score, but I think that the players try to do their best and create moments that we want to see."
Again Pocognoli called for patience and the time which Robertson says Scotland do not have.
"The more we have games together, the more we will try to fix these things," the head coach said. "We have a lot of good response from this camp and it's good for the future as well."
But whatever Pocognoli's selling, former Scotland winger Pat Nevin isn't buying.
"If I'm ever in trouble and I need a PR man, I'm getting him because he's absolutely good at it," he said on Sportsound.
"He's certainly a glass-half-full person. You can talk away any moment and say it's just a moment, but it's four moments, five moments, six moments.
"A really horrible thing in that situation is that if I am running the SFA, I'd be asking the players what they think and just saying 'tell us the truth... are you backing us?'
"If a couple of the main ones say 'we're not sure of the decision-making' then I think it's got to that stage."
Fraser: Utter shambles. Embarassing. How can players who play for so called "big" clubs look like they've never seen a football before when they put on a Scotland shirt?
Matt: Six games. Six poor results. Our ranking will tank. And all Clarke's good work will be undone. It's time to admit Mulholland got it wrong. Sometimes you don't need data and metrics to see the simple solution. Poco no more.
Shirleyanne: All these comments about how rubbish we are I would like to know if they are the same people who when we play well are getting in touch praising the team?? The manager needs time, the players need time too.. Yes it's not been great but come on give them a chance and get behind them instead of moaning..
Grant: Pocognoli is the new Russell Martin, talks a good game but is actually clueless and too stubborn to admit his tactics are dire. I did say be careful what you wish for when the gaffer quit in June and this will only end one way so might as well get it done well before March. Someone should call Steve Clarke.
Brett: When you have limited resources like Scotland, you have to utilise them to good effect - take a look at what Michael O'Neil is doing with Northern Ireland, he is getting results. And you can say that Scotland has a better pool of players to choose from than Northern Ireland does, so...

A few short months ago, Craig Mulholland, the Scottish FA's chief football officer, and Ian Maxwell, the association's chief executive, spoke about the worldwide search for a new Scotland head coach.
The data, the metrics, the cosmic input from the analytics company whose input was received at Hampden as if written on tablets of stone.
The process all pointed to Sebastien Pocognoli being their guy. They paraded him around Hampden, told everybody that loads of clubs were on his tail but that they won the chase.
They may, or may not, have mentioned the word 'coup' but that was certainly what their body language was telling you.
For coup, read boo, the sound surely reverberating around the Tartan Army right now after Monday's 4-0 defeat by Switzerland.
Some nonsense has been written about Pocognoli being on twice the salary that Steve Clarke was on, but whatever they're paying him, there's no value in it so far.
Money is a factor here. Clarke's three qualifications brought a rich bounty into the SFA's coffers, many millions even after deductions. That cash gave the association a little more opportunity to do some of the things they want to do in grassroots football.
A world where Scotland miss out on major championships and the financial windfalls that come with qualification is not a place they want to revisit. The next Euros looks like a gimme - almost harder not to qualify than qualify - but the sense of drift in this team is alarming and can't go on much longer.
Mulholland, Maxwell and let's throw SFA president Mike Mulraney into the mix, should be feeling mightily nervous.
Pocognoli wants patience but Scotland 'don't have time' says Robertson
Pocognoli's abject Scotland suffer 4-0 Nations League defeat in Switzerland
Robertson eclipses Dalglish to become Scotland's most capped man
Most people understood that Pocognoli needed time, but implicit in that understanding was a need to see something developing under him, a burgeoning style of play, some positives here and there, a few signs that even though things might not be great today or tomorrow, they're inching in the right direction.
There's been none of that. Decent players look lost. Pocognoli's system has made Scotland a disjointed soft touch. Structural discipline collapses too often. Players charge forward and leave space in behind. He wants hard pressing and maximum intensity, but his players don't look capable of providing it.
In six games they have scored five goals - two from the penalty spot. Promises of jam tomorrow are not cutting it. People can see a team on the slide.
In Switzerland, there was a drubbing that piles the heat on the Belgian, on the people who appointed him and on the players, too.
If the chaos on the field wasn't a bad enough look for Pocognoli, then some of the words said in the wake of this objectionable 4-0 pummelling to a Switzerland B side playing in third gear only made things worse.
Andy Robertson, on the night he became Scotland's most capped player in history, delivered a damning riff that sounded strongly like a commentary on this coaching regime and this set of players.
In his stead, John McGinn did much the same thing. "You don't get time" was the gist. Who doesn't get time?
Robertson and McGinn didn't lay it on the line, but their thoughts resembled distress flares. These Scotland players can be overhyped, but they are better than some of the nonsense they dished up in St Gallen.
More than one former Scotland international reckoned they saw players not exactly busting a gut out there. These guys know the tell-tale signs.
Some private conversations between the SFA hierarchy and the senior operators in this team need to take place. What were they suggesting in the post-match? What are they really thinking?
An honesty session behind closed doors needs to take place long before the qualification campaign for the next Euros begins in March.
Pocognoli comes across as a good person: open, communicative, passionate and hard-working.
He also appears stubborn in the way he sets up his team, a system that is so easily exploited by more experienced coaches, people like Switzerland boss Murat Yakin, who was missing a battalion of heavy hitters and yet still won this game at a canter.
Yakin started six players who had six caps or fewer to their name - three of them scored.
McGinn said later that Scotland were in this movie before in the early days of Clarke's tenure, mentioning the 4-0 loss to Russia in 2019 - four goals conceded in 27 minutes.
The difference between Clarke and Pocognoli is obvious. Clarke had vast experience and the nous to fix the problems. Pocognoli is a young coach with no such back story, no such track record in turning bad situations into good.
Pocognoli said later that people should look beyond the result, to the "attitude of the players" who were at times "brilliant, brave and on the front foot".
He argued that 4-0 wasn't a true reflection of the game, referring to the glaring misses by Lewis Ferguson and Scott McTominay. Scotland were 3-0 down at the time. He didn't think the loss had anything to do with a system or a lack of confidence or a lack of belief.
Not many fans were buying what he was selling. Listening to some of his players, you doubted that they were buying it either.
After the home loss to Slovenia, Robertson said his team had been "out-played" and "out-fought." There were some other comments made after the desperately stodgy 2-1 win over North Macedonia on Friday. On Monday, it cranked up another level.
McGinn was asked if he felt Scotland were on the right path. "Impossible for me to say yes," he replied. It was hard to listen to what the players were trying to say and conclude that everybody's on the same page in this set-up.
Intransigence is not a good characteristic for any manager. In recent times we've seen a few bosses at big clubs who were wedded to their principles. Russell Martin and Wilfried Nancy didn't last long at Rangers and Celtic.
Clarke had an instinctive understanding of that and pragmatism was his way of taking his team forward, difficult yard by difficult yard. Rigid idealism is not a sensible way to operate, but Pocognoli has gone down that road in his first six games.
It's a dead-end down there. He needs to turn back and find another way while he still can. If he still can.

As Zeki Amdouni arrowed in second-string Switzerland's fabulous fourth goal, the body language of dejected Scotland duo Andy Robertson and Ryan Christie was telling.
The captain's record-breaking 103rd cap played out in cruel fashion. Suited and booted for the occasion, with commemorative boots and a personalised armband, there was no cause for celebration as Robertson was, yet again, wheeled out afterwards to make sense of the 4-0 scudding in St Gallen.
So too were John McGinn and Kieran Tierney. Billy Gilmour, who has also surpassed the half-century caps landmark, also did a bit of talking. Substitute Christie was spared this time.
After a result of this kind, rounding up a humdrum maiden campaign for manager Sebastien Pocognoli, it's necessary for the experienced heads to front-up.
When he named his first squad, so much kudos was thrown the Belgian's way for breaking away from the norm and bleeding in the stars of tomorrow.
But such young and bright lights were only allowed to shine on the bench, at best, as Pocognoli turned to the tried and tested.
As former Scotland international Leanne Crichton said on BBC Scotland's Sportscene: "There's a reliance still, clearly, on that key core of Scotland players.
"And, when you listen to it post-match, they sound dejected, they don't sound that confident about what is going on. It is a difficult place to be."
Pocognoli's abject Scotland suffer 4-0 Nations League defeat in Switzerland
St Gallen was a mighty troubling place for the Scots on Monday night.
The calm, picturesque city was invaded by coral shirt and kilt-clad Scotsmen from Sunday, but they - and their heroes on the pitch - couldn't wait to get out of the place after a poor showing at the Sitterstadion.
A narrow half-time deficit turned into a drubbing on the final whistle, at which the Scots remained goalless despite a handful of hopeful situations.
McGinn, the scorer of Scotland's past three goals, directed a weak header goalbound before the break, while Scott McTominay - nearly one year on from his Hampden heroics against Denmark - missed a couple of glaring opportunities.
"If McTominay is not operating at his highest level for the national team, there is an impact on results," Crichton said.
"If McGinn doesn't produce the goods on an evening, we're in trouble.
"If Gilmour and Ferguson in the middle of the pitch [don't perform], if Christie doesn't come on with an impact, we are [too reliant].
"And that's where you need to breed a different confidence in a different group."
Kieron Bowie, who many hoped would be in from the off, came on just before the hour mark and got right in about it, as is the striker's style.
Winger Ben Gannon-Doak, dropped for Aaron Hickey, did come on after the wing-back ended up going off with an apparent hamstring injury before Kristi Montgomery was handed a debut with five minutes to go.
Wide-men Findlay Curtis and Josh McPake were left on the bench, again. Robbie Ure didn't make either matchday squad this camp.
All three natural wingers excite supporters, even if they have only been handed a matter of minutes, but Pocognoli's system does not suit them.
That said, the players insist they're invested in the project.
"We have to believe that we're going in the right direction," Robertson added after a beyond-deflating defeat.
"Of course, there's going to be humps in the road, but when I look back on Steve Clarke's opening six games - I can't remember all the results but - I don't think everyone was shouting and screaming about Steve Clarke's Scotland after the first six games.
"We're trying to get a team together and we're trying to build a good atmosphere off the pitch.
"People wanted change within the squad. We've done that change and now we need to try and integrate the squad.
"We need to get close as a squad again, integrate the young players, make them feel a part of it, make them step up - it's for us to try and help them do it."

Declan Rice has agreed a new long term-contract at Arsenal so can he continue to go from strength to strength? Jack Wilshere, his former team-mate at West Ham, tells Sky Sports Rice is "definitely in the conversation as one of the best midfielders in the world"
Arsenal's Kroenke family owners tend not to get involved in transfer dealings. But when it came to Declan Rice, and the prospect of spending £100m on a player for the first time, they needed to be sure that it was a sensible investment.
So, in the conference room at Arsenal's training ground, co-chair Josh Kroenke asked to be walked through the deal by Mikel Arteta, former sporting director Edu, then executive vice-chair Tim Lewis and now chief executive officer Richard Garlick.
"My eyebrows raised because I didn't know if we were in that phase just yet to go after a player like that," Kroenke recalled. He wanted to know what he would bring and how Arteta would use him. He wanted reassurance that he could hit the ground running.
Kroenke left the meeting in no doubt about the deal, either financially or in footballing terms. A club-record approach to West Ham was greenlit and Rice has of course gone on to prove an inspired addition, his new deal reflecting his importance.
"Declan Rice, we got him half price," is the refrain among Arsenal supporters. A player instrumental in their Premier League title success, who insisted "it's not done", then did more than anyone to drive them over the line, is now tied down for his peak years.
He has brought Arsenal even more than the club anticipated, arriving as a No 6 before being unshackled as a rampaging No 8, then reverting to a deeper role this season.
He scores, creates and dominates physically. His deadly set-piece delivery, honed to a world-class level, is another weapon.
"He is becoming a total player," said Arteta, who has even called on him at right-back. Of course, Rice filled in admirably in that role. "A total player has to be able to do as many things as possible and he has the capacity to do that," added Arteta.
Rice's adaptability and willingness to evolve his game have been themes of his time at Arsenal. The same traits were apparent to those who worked with him at West Ham, where he made an instant impression on his former team-mate Jack Wilshere.
"I love Declan, first of all a person," Wilshere tells Sky Sports. "I could see that straight away when I went in. He was very humble, his eyes were open, he wanted to learn, he would ask the right questions, and he just went from strength to strength.
"His footballing ability speaks for itself, but I wouldn't say he's someone who it came naturally to. He had to work on his right foot, on his left foot. But physically, he was always a beast and that would help him get out of certain situations."
Wilshere also noted the leadership qualities that have come to the fore at Arsenal. "Even when I went there and he was 19 or 20 and finding his way in the team, he had natural leadership and a natural aura about him that you could see," he says.
Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player
"He has a good understanding as well. When you look at players making big moves now, for me, one of the most important things around it is timing. I think Dec got his timing right.
"He spent a good few years at West Ham becoming a hero, becoming an important member of that team, trying to get that team up the table to finish high as possible. He won a trophy with them, and then he decided to go and compete for bigger things."
Wilshere and Rice crossed paths again following his move to Arsenal, where Wilshere, now head coach of Luton Town, was working as an academy coach and shadowing his old team-mate Arteta.
"I know how important he was to Mikel at that time when Mikel brought him in, and how he was going to be that shining light of the team who would always be present," he says.
"That's another thing that's really impressive about him: his robustness. He plays every single game. He dominates every single game physically."
Rice's record bears it out. Last season was his most demanding yet as he made 55 appearances in all competitions for Arsenal, many of them while managing hamstring nerve pain, before making a further eight for England at the World Cup during the summer.
He is an incredible athlete who continues to show remarkable resistance to injury. He has only missed five out of 119 Premier League games since his arrival at Arsenal. Only four outfield players have played more minutes in the competition in that timeframe.
His reliability is invaluable to Arteta and Rice continues to find ways to improve. Having moved back to the base of midfield this term, switching to the right side of the pivot to accommodate Myles Lewis-Skelly and Bruno Guimaraes, he has become notably more incisive with his passes.
His total of five assists is the highest of any Premier League player this season and it is notable that all of them have come in open-play.
According to Opta, Rice ranks second among Premier League players - and top among midfielders - for line-breaking passes this season, behind only Jan Paul van Hecke. He also ranks second only to Martin Odegaard for line-breaking passes in the final third.
A player once criticised for sideways passing is now averaging nearly twice as many line-breaking passes than last season, showing clear development in yet another area of his game.
The hope for Arsenal is that Rice will continue to unlock more levels after committing his future to the club. That is certainly the expectation from those who know him.
"I actually think there's more to come from Dec," adds Wilshere. "I've said it for a few years now. To be fair, he has started to add goals, but I still think he can add more with his physical ability, with his ability to strike the ball off his left foot, right foot.
"But he's already a top player and definitely in the conversation as one of the best midfielders in the world."

As he prepares to depart for Manchester United, the outgoing US coach held court on a number of topics, including what he’d change about soccer in America
O utgoing US head coach Mauricio Pochettino and former Manchester City head coach Pep Guardiola have a long, storied past. The two faced each other as players, when Guardiola was at Barcelona and Pochettino was making his name across town at Espanyol. They faced each other 22 times as managers in the Premier League and the two share a mutual respect – and intensity – when it comes to their approach to playing and coaching alike.
So when Guardiola visited Yankee Stadium in September to serve as New York City FC’s pre-match hype man before their rivalry match with Red Bull New York, Pochettino – in town anyways to scout the match – made it a point to sit with him during the game. He brought along his assistant coach and confidant Jesús Pérez, and US Soccer CEO and secretary general JT Batson.
“You know what I noticed?” Pochettino asked, smiling as he recounted the story during a meeting with reporters on Monday. “[Guardiola had a] good relationship with JT.”
Back then, Pochettino didn’t seem to be going anywhere. Only a month earlier, he’d signed a four-year contract to guide the US through the 2030 World Cup. Guardiola was, and still is, in the middle of a year-long sabbatical from coaching. He remains the federation’s white whale, often mentioned in the same breath as the US job over the past decade-plus but just as quickly dismissed as a pipe dream.
Just three months after taking in that game at Yankee Stadium, Pochettino is on his way to Manchester United and Guardiola has once again found himself at the center of the rumor mill, with reports suggesting that he and US Soccer are set for exploratory talks.
On Monday, Pochettino was asked what he’d tell the Barcelona and Manchester City legend if he was asked for his opinion on the US job.
“Take it,” Pochettino said, flatly. “Why? Because it’s a perfect moment to arrive at the federation. Everything is on the right path, in the right direction. Of course, take it. Of course, you are going to find really good players, good people – the players can fit his style.”
Guardiola was one of many topics the Argentinian manager covered during the roundtable, which lasted about an hour. At times defiant, at times emotional and cycling through Spanish and English, Pochettino spoke of his potential legacy at US Soccer, what lies ahead for him at United and how he views soccer in America as a whole.
However you assess his results, one of the inarguable successes of the Pochettino era are the relatively unheralded players whose status has risen over his tenure. The Argentine cited defender Alex Freeman and midfielder Sebastian Berhalter as two such examples, both of whom were playing in MLS when making their national team debuts under Pochettino and both now playing in Europe. Asked how he assesses players to add to the national team, and how he compares players across different leagues and playing styles, Pochettino insisted that the level of competition matters less than individual form.
“You need to project the individual player,” Pochettino said. “Because he’s playing well, the level is no issue. That player can be good, like Freeman, like Sebastian. That is the example, and I think that is so important. There is talent everywhere … This one is one of the things that we learn – all [of us], we were young and then we start to be a coach, no? That we cannot make a mistake [and] measure the level of the player because of the level of the league.”
With the US being his first international job, there were some doubts going in about how Pochettino would adapt to coaching without daily contact with his players and staff.
“I am ready [to return]. This is what I miss a little bit. I miss to be, every day, with something here,” Pochettino said. “Guardiola asked me when I was at the game, he said, ‘Oh, you don’t want to come back to the Premier League?’ I said, ‘No, I’m happy here.’ [He said] ‘Yeah, but you don’t miss, every day, to…’ I say, ‘A little bit, yes, because you think now today, and then we have December camp against Jamaica for the MLS [players in the pool]. But after, you need to wait [until] March. What do you do? You need to watch games, you need to travel – administrative things. That is nice, it’s good. But every day, to be involved: press conference, training, everything … this type of possibility, like with United, you say yes. I want that. I want to prove myself again.”
But what did Pochettino think of his maiden international job?
“I like and not like,” he said. “I like because it provides you the possibility to manage your time, to be busy, but at the same time, be free and to have some time with your family. Now, I have a grandchild, and [number] two is coming. You can share the life with your people. But now, ciao, because now is [gestures] tra-tra-tra-tra-tra . It’s impossible to spend time with the people you want.”
In the grand scheme of international football, the US national team coaching job has never been close to the top of the list of most desirable destinations. Pochettino’s hire was seen as a possible sign that could be changing. Now, after nearly two years in the position, Pochettino believes it has.
“The vision from Europe, I promise it is completely different after the World Cup,” Pochettino said. “Now, being head coach of the USA is more prestigious. If Manchester United, or Real Madrid, or Barcelona is coming for the US coach, if you start to think about that, if you are another coach – maybe [Antonio] Conte, someone else, you say ‘oh, this is a great opportunity.’ [In my case], ‘Oh, Pochettino, from Chelsea he goes to the US? And now to Manchester United.’
Pochettino has coached some of the most famous players and clubs in the world, giving him a unique perspective on how soccer has developed in the US. Pochettino stopped short of prescribing neat solutions to improve the sport, though.
“I think that business [and] the sport, is [done] in a holistic way. Everything is important, and you cannot pick one. You cannot change one [thing], and that can change everything,” he said. “I think it’s a little bit of everything that you need to change. If you adjust this, you need to adjust this. The balance of the thing changes if you touch here, that will force you to touch all the areas in soccer here, or in the world To find the good balance, no? A process of little by little, is all that we made in these last two years. I think it’s the beginning of [a process]. If that has continuity, it’s the beginning of the new soccer in the USA that can be.
“I think that is, for me, the beginning of the change for the future: that idea that the American player can be very good, can be very competitive. The talent is here; it’s so powerful in this country. I think that is why I feel proud. Maybe that was our job, because I don’t believe in coincidence. That has happened because something needed to happen. Now the tough job is done. Maybe now [the United job] is my reward because of this tough job.”

Mauricio Pochettino was appointed United States head coach in 2024
Mauricio Pochettino says he would tell Pep Guardiola to take the United States job if the former Manchester City manager was offered it.
Pochettino, 54, is leaving his role as the US men's team head coach to become Manchester United 's new manager from 18 November, after signing a two-and-a-half-year contract until June 2029.
He takes charge of his final game with the US on Tuesday when they face Haiti in the second leg of the Concacaf Nations League quarter-finals in Cincinnati, Ohio.
Guardiola, 55, is taking a one-year sabbatical after stepping down as City boss in May.
Reports have suggested Guardiola could be a contender to succeed Pochettino in the US, although there has been no formal contact between the Spaniard and the United States Soccer Federation.
Pochettino told reporters on Monday his advice to Guardiola would be to take the role, "because it's a perfect moment to arrive at the federation."
Tearful Pochettino on 'difficult' decision to leave USA for Man Utd
The Argentine added: "Everything is on the right path, in the right direction.
"Of course, take it. Of course, you are going to find really good players, good people - the players can fit his style."
Former Tottenham and Chelsea boss Pochettino is replacing Michael Carrick at United. Carrick was sacked as head coach last week with the club in the relegation zone in 18th place.
His long-time assistant Jesus Perez, goalkeeping coach Toni Jimenez and athletic coach, 31-year-old son Sebastiano Pochettino, arrived in England following the US's 6-0 first-leg victory over Haiti in Miami last weekend.
Pochettino's first test back in the Premier League is an away trip to Anfield to face fourth-placed Liverpool on Sunday.
"They are in advance, they are preparing all there, because Wednesday when we will arrive, it is going to be non-stop," he said.
"For me, it's not difficult, I think we are well prepared to switch quick."

Diego Gomez's shot against Crystal Palace soars over Walter Benitez
David Beckham's goal from the halfway line against Wimbledon in 1996 is one of football's iconic moments.
It helped to catapult the Manchester United midfielder to global stardom and remains a staple of highlight reels.
The impudence to shoot from such a distance highlighted the exceptional talent and character of the future England captain.
Premier League players are now trying their luck from long range more regularly, testing their instinct, precision and technique.
Diego Gomez's stunning 51-metre (56-yard) strike for Brighton against Crystal Palace last month added to the spectacular list in the Premier League, while players in the EFL and FA Cup have contributed their own.
There have already been 19 attempts from over 50 metres this season, on course to beat last season's Premier League total of 26.
Of the 2,733 shots in the Premier League this term, 0.7% of them have come from over halfway - up on 0.3% over the course of last season.
This sample size is admittedly small. And in the case of goals scored from distance lower down the football pyramid, this is data that isn't readily available.
But why are we seeing a growing number of shots being taken from such extravagant distance?
Gomez tried to score from deep in his own half during Brighton 's 2-0 win at Sunderland on 10 October.
A week later, he beat Walter Benitez with the longest-range goal in the Premier League since Wayne Rooney's 57.6m strike for Everton against West Ham in 2017.
The Paraguayan took advice from Lionel Messi, when the pair were at Inter Miami, to always look to play the ball forward to another level.
It is not just Premier League players who are trying their luck from outrageous distances.
Charlie McNeill scored from halfway for Crewe in their recent 2-1 FA Cup win against AFC Wimbledon.
The on-loan Sheffield Wednesday forward, who played once for Manchester United before leaving Old Trafford in 2024, beat goalkeeper Joe Bursik to open the scoring.
Having done it while at Manchester City and Manchester United 's academies, the 23-year-old felt his latest attempt was instinctive.
He told BBC Sport: "Goalies nowadays are always quite high up the pitch - playing a sweeper-keeper role - and I always have a thought if I ever got into that situation to have a go.
"You see it more and more. I had the opportunity so I thought: 'Why not have a go?'
"It was one of those goals. I turned and saw him off his line and in that split-second made the decision to shoot.
"I knew I caught it sweetly and I was following it the whole way in so I knew it had a good chance, but as the keeper was going back I thought he was going to get it.
"When I watched it back it dropped quite early, but as it was getting closer and closer I thought it was going to go over because it went quite high but it dropped in."
Crewe Alexandra's Charlie McNeill talking about the rise in halfway line goals
McNeill joins a growing number of players to have scored from the halfway line or inside their own half over the past 18 months.
Preston Fearon, now on loan at Forest Green, scored two goals from around the halfway line for West Ham Under-21s in their win against Burnley last month.
Gbemi Arubi was barely a stride over the halfway line when he scored for Burton against Peterborough in October.
Last season, Abdul Fatawu (Leicester), Ryan Ledson (Huddersfield), Reyes Cleary (Barnsley), Regan Hendry (Mansfield) and Sammy Braybrooke (Newport) all scored from the halfway line or inside their own half in the EFL.
Two years ago, Chelsea 's Moises Caicedo scored from the centre circle against Bournemouth.
Is it all about the goalkeeper's position, as they stand higher up the pitch to either stop opposition attacks or get their own team moving?
"You've got to execute it properly, but it plays a big part. Most keepers are like that, high out the net, because we are playing over the top so they are there first, to get the ball," said McNeill.
"I have always had it in my head and have tried it a couple of times. Although it's not like I do my homework and see he is always off his line. It's one of those instinctive moments."
Paul Robinson scored two goals in his career, one for Tottenham and one for Leeds
Asmir Begovic holds the record for the longest-range Premier League goal when the goalkeeper scored from 95.7m for Stoke against Southampton in 2013.
Two other goalkeepers have scored from their own half: Tim Howard for Everton against Bolton in 2012 and Paul Robinson, who netted for Tottenham against Watford in 2007.
Yet they were flukes rather than by design - similar to Barrow goalkeeper Ben Winterbottom's goal from his own half in their 3-0 National League win at Gateshead on Saturday.
Robinson, who also scored for Leeds against Swindon in 2004 , external , feels conceding from distance is now a risk managers are willing to take.
The former England international said: "We've seen the game evolve in the way where the goalkeeper becomes a key figure in starting a pattern of play. The manager wants the goalkeeper at the base of the back three, four or five.
"But then also we're seeing a lot more teams playing with a higher line and the goalkeeper then has to take a higher line of starting position to read the through ball.
"When your team are playing a high line, you obviously have to be further up the field and you're concentrating on where your defensive line is, as opposed to where the football is at times.
"It's one of those things modern-day managers are willing to accept if and when it does happen, because of the way they want their goalkeeper to play.
"We see so many managers come out now and say: 'It's OK. I'm quite happy with them making mistakes. This is the way I want them to play. Blame me because that's what I've asked them to do.'
With attackers aware of the higher starting position of opposing keepers - a result of teams pressing high - and likely to have been encouraged by the success of other long-range efforts across football, attempts from extreme distance are becoming more frequent in the Premier League this season.
The conversion of efforts from more than 50 metres have increased too - up to 5.3% this season, compared to 1.1% across the previous three seasons combined, with Gomez's strike the first Premier League goal scored from over 50 metres since the 2023-24 season.
It's a small sample size, so more time is required for clearer trends, at least in the Premier League to be established.
But with more long shots being taken and keepers starting higher, there is a suggestion (and hope) we may see more Goal of the Season contenders before the term is out.

Izzy Goodwin has scored three goals in five WSL appearances for London City
London City Lionesses forward Izzy Goodwin has been named in the England squad for the first time for the World Cup qualifying play-off against Ukraine.
The 23-year-old has been in great form this month and scored in front of England manager Sarina Wiegman at Emirates Stadium on Sunday in a 1-1 draw with Arsenal.
"We have always see her as a huge talent with potential," Wiegman told BBC Radio 5 Live.
"I think London City are developing really well in the games they have showed. She is tall and can head a ball attacking-wise, but also defending.
"She is really quick with her feet and can score goals. I really want to see her in our environment, what she can bring and how close she is to the level that we expect."
There is also a first call-up for goalkeeper Katie Cox, on loan at Nottingham Forest from Chelsea, while Manchester United midfielder Ella Toone returns.
Manchester City duo Niamh Charles and Alex Greenwood, who is injured, are among those to miss out.
The Lionesses play Ukraine in Spain on 1 December before hosting them at Wembley on 5 December. The winner qualifies for next year's Women's World Cup.
"We know what's at stake in these games and our focus is on producing two strong performances to secure our place at the World Cup," said Wiegman.
"We have worked hard to put ourselves in this position and now we have to finish the job.
"Ukraine will provide a challenge and we will prepare with the same focus and determination that we always do."
Chelsea defender Lucy Bronze could make her 150th appearance at Wembley in the second leg.
England travel to Pinatar, Spain a few days before the first leg and opted not to play a friendly match during this extended international break.
"The first part of the block we are [at St George's Park]. We have training sessions and a period of time where we can do some tactical stuff," added Wiegman.
"We also selected more players so that helps us create situations where we can train things and everyone is important. I'm really excited to get ready for these games."

England manager Sarina Wiegman has named a 25-player squad for next month’s World Cup qualifying play-off against Ukraine; Ella Toone and Aggie Beever-Jones return to the squad
Sarina Wiegman has named 25 players for England’s decisive FIFA Women’s World Cup play-off against Ukraine, with Ella Toone and Aggie Beever-Jones returning to the squad.
Toone was initially excluded from the camp to face Greece in October with Wiegman saying that she had not "played to her potential". She earned a recall following an injury to Lucy Bronze, having impressed with her reaction to the setback.
Chloe Kelly was also a notable absence from the last squad, but this time misses out due to a hamstring problem that has kept her out since the end of September.
Beever-Jones returns having last featured for the Lionesses in their 6-1 victory over Ukraine back in March. She takes the place of Chelsea team-mate Lauren James who is sidelined. Grace Clinton also earns a recall.

There is also an opportunity for Bronze to make history by becoming just the third woman to reach 150 caps. She currently sits on 148, with injury forcing her to miss the chance in the two-legged tie against Greece.
England are one victory away from booking their ticket to next summer's World Cup in Brazil, with Ukraine standing between them and qualification in the second round of the play-offs.

"We know what's at stake in these games and our focus is on producing two strong performances to secure our place at the World Cup," Wiegman said.

The two-match tie will mark England's first outing since head coach Wiegman committed her future to the national team by agreeing a contract extension through to Euro 2029 .
“We are in conversation all the time. The FA are still happy with me and I think they are trailblazers for the women’s game and a great federation to work for," Wiegman said when asked about her extension.
"That’s really important for me of course. Also the connection between the staff and the players and my colleagues in the FA is still very good. There are great challenges too in the nearest future and but also further down the line.
"We have the World Cup coming which takes us back to the Ukraine games that we have to win. Then we have to qualify for the Olympics and then the Euros in Germany."

T here may have been an Mbappé on the pitch – Ethan, the younger brother of Kylian, with whom he shares a near-identical gait – but by the end there was only one precocious talent on the lips of those watching England overcome France in their under-21s clash. Max Dowman had done it again, lighting up another game, this time in filthy conditions at Ashton Gate. It was fitting he had the final say in a 3-2 win. The noise that accompanied his match-winning goal? Well, beyond the palpable excitement in the stands in Bristol, that would be the sound of the teenager sending yet another record tumbling.
Which one takes your fancy? Take your pick. At 14, playing for Arsenal’s under-19s, he became the Uefa Youth League’s youngest goalscorer. This time last year, after taking to the field at Slavia Prague aged 15 and 308 days, Dowman became the youngest player to feature in the Champions League. In March, six months on from his professional debut, he became the Premier League’s youngest goalscorer. He is the youngest player to earn a Premier League winner’s medal. Last month he was presented with three Guinness World Records.
In scoring his first under-21s goal, in the penultimate minute of regular time, Dowman eclipsed Jude Bellingham to become the team’s youngest scorer at 16 years and 320 days, three days after surpassing the Real Madrid midfielder’s record as the under-21s’ youngest player. Bellingham was almost four months older than Dowman when he scored his first goal for the age group, in September 2020. Bellingham made only four appearances for the under-21s, a result of being fast-tracked into the senior team, and Dowman could emulate him again, though he is expected to feature in next summer’s Under-21 European Championship in Albania and Serbia.
The common view from coaches and teammates, and something stressed by Lee Carsley, the under-21s head coach, is that it is easy to forget Dowman is a month shy of his 17th birthday. Against France, it was also extremely easy to overlook that this was Dowman’s first start for the under-21s, after a substitute appearance against Portugal last Friday. His first action set the tone on Monday, using his body to box off the ball then jinking up the right flank, zipping it through the legs of Dayann Methalie before skating forward and sending the Sunderland left-back juddering on to his backside.
Dowman exhibited plenty of neat touches, a couple of effortless first-time passes, but those who have watched him develop say his work rate and willingness to do the other side of the game is one of his biggest strengths. “We look at Max and see how good he is on the ball, how attacking he is, but I thought he was outstanding off the ball,” Carsley said, presumably thinking of the moment Dowman scampered deep into his own half to intercept a stray France pass. He was not finished after scoring either. At one point he had five blue shirts haring after him as he stormed into the France half and, seconds later, his quick feet lured opposition captain, Nathan Zézé, into a foul on the edge of the box.
Dowman is among the next wave of players pushing to step up to Thomas Tuchel’s squad, perhaps at its forefront. It is a well-trodden path and the current crop need not look too far for inspiration. Elliot Anderson and Jarell Quansah, both of whom started England’s triumph at the last under-21 Euros in Bratislava, began Sunday’s memorable victory for the seniors in Madrid . Jobe Bellingham and Josh King are the latest players to make the transition into Tuchel’s squad and more will follow.
Jack Hinshelwood and Trey Nyoni, of Brighton and Liverpool respectively, impressed at the base of midfield and the 19-year-old Mikey Moore, another to score on his first start for the under-21s, shone down the left flank, opening the scoring. The Everton midfielder Harrison Armstrong entered as a substitute and supplied Dowman’s winner, and Armstrong’s clubmate Tyrique George also showed promise after replacing Moore. Archie Gray captained the under-21s against Portugal but did not feature on Monday, with Carsley revealing he has spoken to the Tottenham midfielder about Scotland wanting him to switch allegiance . “I just said to him: ‘Keep me in the picture, if it’s something that you were thinking of,’” Carsley said. “I think Archie is very connected to our pathway.”
England’s budding talent is not confined to the under-21s. Carsley took a closer look at Brian Madjo, the imposing 17-year-old striker who scored on his Aston Villa debut in the Super Cup in August, the Manchester United defender Ayden Heaven and the West Brom forward Jimmy-Jay Morgan, who signed from Chelsea in the summer, before his squad departed for Bristol last week, the trio joining the under-21s for four days of training at St George’s Park.
Dowman, after two under-21 appearances comprising a total of a little more than 120 minutes, is putting the squeeze on. “Max is doing something special for his age and he is pushing people a lot older than him,” said Moore, who is on loan from Tottenham at Köln and hopes to face his idol Harry Kane and Bayern Munich on Friday. “He’s a top kid. You kind of forget how old he is. My little brother is 17 and he [Dowman] feels older to me than my little brother … He has been top and everywhere he goes, he just takes that next step.”

Scotland ended their Nations League campaign with a 4-0 defeat to Switzerland; Sebastien Pocognoli has won two of his first six games as head coach; the Scots are set to find themselves in pot three for next month's Euro 2028 qualifying draw
A year is a long time in football and that is certainly the case when it comes to Scotland's fortunes.
From a historic night against Denmark as the long wait to return to the World Cup finally ended, to a bruising 4-0 defeat to Switzerland at the end of a frustrating Nations League campaign. The contrast is stark.
A second-half collapse against a second-string Swiss side in St Gallen condemned the Scots to their heaviest loss since their 5-1 thrashing by Germany at Euro 2024.
After also leading Scotland to back-to-back Euros, Steve Clarke was always going to be a hard act to follow. After just six games, some of the Tartan Army have already seen enough from Sebastien Pocognoli.
The new head coach managed two wins against North Macedonia in Group B1. The third-place finish means Scotland will be in pot three when the qualifying draw is made for Euro 2028 on December 6, meaning a potentially more challenging campaign.
Pocognoli wants time, something even his captain Andy Robertson said you do not get in international football.
Pocognoli has consistently stressed the need for patience as he tries to implement a more attack-minded style.
He favours a back three featuring wing-backs, with two attacking midfielders or a central playmaker supporting a single striker as he looks to press high up the pitch.
Pacy winger Ben Gannon-Doak has frequently been deployed at right wing-back in this system, but his natural attacking fair is being limited by the defensive demands that brings.
While Clarke did use a back five in his early tenure to try and accomodate both Andy Roberston and John McGinn, he favoured a more traditional back four.
His teams were not always entertaining to watch, but they did get the job done. Most of the time.
The question for Pocognoli is, should he stick to his principles or look at what his predecessor did to bring the highs the Tartan Army had been missing?
After two camps and six games, any grace period the Belgian had is over.
Time with the players is something international managers do not have, but Pocognoli has already had more than some.
The elongated international window between September and October, followed by the most recent camp means he has had 24 days with his squad. That is equivalent to what a Scottish Premiership side has between day one of pre-season and their first game in the League Cup group stages.
Andy Robertson became Scotland's most capped men's player against Switzerland, but there was not much for the captain to celebrate.
"That cannot happen in international football," he told BBC Scotland after the match.
"I don't think you've got time in international football, you have to do it. These supporters who travel everywhere, are they going to give us time? No. Are the people inside Hampden going to give us time? No. Are the people outside Hampden, who are going to be critical and rightly so? No.
"We don't have time, the players do not have time, we have got to step up."
John McGinn echoed his skipper when asked if Scotland were on the right path: "Well, obviously the trajectory of the results means it's impossible for me to say yes."
James Scott from the Football Park Scotland podcast speaking on Sky Sports News:
"It's the early days and the players. It'll take time for us to maybe get going on this but that can't be the detriment of results.
"We can accept a poor performance against Macedonia, still getting the win, but coming away against Switzerland, it's a much tougher task and I think we could save face a bit by maybe just making a few adjustments.
"Losing against Switzerland is not a bad thing but to ship four goals in the manner we did with the lack of fight, the jury's out on the formation now. It's starting to frustrate people.
"We've got two friendlies now in March, Euro qualifiers starting next year. If things don't change in the friendlies, the frustration really will start to build because you don't get a lot of time in international football and I think mistakes do cost you more.
"We can't make amends for last night until then and then the qualifiers come around and there's really no room to slip up there because you don't want to be relying on the sort of safety net of being a host to get in.
"We would like to qualify and we don't want to miss out on a tournament that's happening in our own back garden and not being there."
The next international break is not until March, with two friendlies before the Euro 2028 qualifying campaign kicks off.
Robertson admitted the long wait is "not a good thing" as they look to regroup after the Nations League disappointment.
While that means no time on the pitch with his players, Pocognoli will have time to assess his squad and tactics. If the Scottish FA decides he is still the right man to lead the national team to their next major tournament.
